metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of Be a Better Landlord, Ashley Kerr sits down with Abi Horton, founder of Aros, to talk about one of the biggest overlooked opportunities for landlords: midterm rentals.

Abi breaks down what midterm rentals are, how they differ from short-term and long-term rentals, and why monthly rentals are becoming more important for landlords in 2026. She explains how relocation companies, traveling professionals, and insurance displacement housing create opportunities for landlords to fill vacancies with longer, more stable bookings.

Whether you own a long-term rental, short-term rental, or vacant property, this episode will help you understand how midterm rentals could become a powerful part of your rental strategy.

Learn more about Abi Horton and Aros:
Website: www.stayarros.com

So, it was reaching out to them, finding out if they had any need for where my property was, and I found that in building these relationships that they were asking me if I knew anybody that had something somewhere else. And I didn't have the properties, but it led me to turn to my communities and my network and the people that I knew, say, "Hey, anybody have something in Austin, Texas or, you know, Virginia or wherever it was." And being able to pair up those people and it just kind of snowballed from there. And Abby, how do you find a relocation company? Is this like a simple Google search or how does someone connect with them? Yeah, kind of. I mean, it's really just about kind of doing the research. I take opportunities when I get them. So, when I get inquiries on my own properties, you know, I ask questions, gather information to see where I can help. You know, maybe I can speak to the company of the person that's inquiring about my property and and ask if we can help them with other searches or, you know, just pulling the threads and uh you know, following down the rabbit hole to see who's the person that we can be the most helpful for. Now, I can expect that these relocation companies want quality properties. They want, you know, quality customer service. So, maybe we can kind of like break down what type of property they are looking for. Like, is it they care about how clean it is? What are they asking from you as the host of this property to provide for them to see if they will even match a family or somebody to go into this property? Yeah, definitely clean. I think that definitely is a basic standard, but yeah, I mean, clean is essential. And as I said earlier, it doesn't have to be furnished. It could be unfurnished. But one of the big things is that the landlord is fast to respond, professional, and easy to work with. You know, all of those things are really key factors in who you're working with cuz at the end of the day, this is a business and it needs to be run like a business relationship. And I like to lead all of my interactions, especially with business, with with value. Like, how can I help you? What can I do that's helpful for you? And and I do that with my rentals, with my business, and and in everything else, too. And I think when you come in it with that mindset, it really helps to just set up the relationships to to work well together. So, I would say you know, that the property can be kind of really any style. A lot of these companies that we work with, sometimes it could be an individual traveling on their own. Sometimes it could be a family of multiple people. So, any size, any style might work, even any location. But having a a landlord that's easy to work with and and professional and and has a professional home and setup is really all that's needed. What about the pricing? Now, are you coming to them and saying this is what my price is or do they come to you and say this is what we're willing to pay? It depends. It depends on the company, it depends on the need. Sometimes they'll come with a budget and I think that there's there's a bit of a misconception between insurance housing and pricing. I think that there's a lot of information out there right now that implies that because it's insurance, it's an endless pot of money and that's just not the case. It's not how it is. So, you know, I think that there are certain things that we can do to price appropriately for what we're offering, especially if you are a long-term landlord where you normally have 12-month leases or more. You can price appropriately for doing a shorter-term lease and having giving them the convenience of offering them a shorter-term lease and that should be priced appropriately for. You know, and we're not expecting a a 12-month lease price for a 3-month lease or a 6-month lease. And also having availability immediately is a convenience that we're offering to people say for insurance relocations. You know, they need something straight away and that sort of thing can also be factored in with price. But sometimes, you know, there is situations where people hear insurance and they think that means endless pots of money and that's just not the case. I I'm going through an insurance claim right now. A tree fell on one of my rental properties and let's just say it's not an endless supply of money they're willing to show up for my new roof. [laughter] Yeah. Yeah. But Abby, you actually cut out a lot of the work that an investor needs to do today to actually match with these relocation companies. You built a platform to actually take you through this process of matching. But before you actually put this platform together, what did it look like a day-to-day as to trying to get in contact with these relocation companies, trying to coordinate and to getting people into your house? Kind of give us a glimpse into what that process was before your platform was built. Yeah, well, I mean, the reason I built the platform was because the process was quite long and time-consuming and I realized, having been on both sides of this transaction, um, as a relocation specialist, it can be really time-consuming to search for the right property because quite often, you know, the location is really the most important thing and the size. They're kind of the two main factors that have to match the criteria. And so, you go to the platforms that are already out there, use the search functions, the filters, zoom in on the map, you know, find something that looks like it might work, and make the call to the landlord or the email or whatever it might be. And sometimes they respond, sometimes they don't, and sometimes they might respond the next day. And and maybe they do call back and they say, "Oh, it's already booked. We just forgot to update our availability." And so, it can be really really time-consuming. And so, you know, obviously we made it work, but naturally I was like, "How can we make this better?" You know, how can we make this more convenient? And so, ultimately the platform was kind of built for relocation companies to be a tool for them to find landlords faster, but that also means that it's a resource for landlords. And so, you know, a place for them to come to specifically be connected with companies that are looking for housing, whether that's for their employees or their clients or whoever that might be, but it's B2B transactions, which makes it a bit cleaner and it's also specifically for mid-term rentals. So, we're not dealing with vacationers or people just coming for a weekend or really high turnover, you know, a couple day stays here and then gaps. You know, we're talking multiple month-long stays where there's no vacancy. There's no turnover. And, you know, I just I it's another thing when you ask if what I love about mid-term rentals, why I love them is that reason, you know, really you can get the maximum amount of cash flow for the minimum amount of effort in terms of the ratio there because they're they're very much easier to manage than short-term rentals and a little bit more work than long-term, but in terms of what you can get back in terms of cash flow, it's much more appealing, I think. Now, Abby, I'm sure everyone listening is chomping at the bit to know, what is the name of this actual platform so they can check it out and maybe give us a little insight into what the process is now as an investor going in and listing your mid-term rental there. Yeah, so the platform is called Aros, which is a r o s, and the website is stayaros.com. It's pretty straightforward functionality-wise. I like to keep things simple. So, in terms of, you know, getting registered and signed up, you can just go to the platform, create a profile, and then create a listing, and it works very much the same way as other platforms out there. You list your bedroom count, your bathrooms, your square footage, any amenities, things that are included, and then it's live. And so, the primary function of this platform is, as I said, it's for relocation companies. So, they can create a housing request for what they need, and they'll be matched using the technology on the platform to any landlord that has a property matching the location and the size, that's the predominant matches. And then, if the landlord has availability, they will be able to submit their property with just a couple of clicks to that housing request. And so, then the relocation specialist can come back and check the properties that have been submitted and be able to communicate directly with the landlord from there. There's got to be people listening there thinking, I have a property that I'm going to turn into a mid-term rental because this seems too good to be true. So, what it, in your opinion, is 2026, the current market conditions, a good time for somebody to pivot their short-term rental or even their long-term rental into a mid-term rental? I think it's only going to come more important to be able to offer monthly rentals. I think as more people travel, as the world keeps going the way it is, I think that a lot of people are traveling with their businesses. You know, we're seeing more insurance claims, you know, from things like hurricanes and floods and fires and things. So, I think having the knowledge of being able to get these opportunities is really important. And that's truly why I created also, is just to share more information with more people because I think there's a lot of people out there that don't know about mid-term rentals. They either don't know how to get started, or they don't know where to find these opportunities. And the problem that I was seeing was that these relocation companies are looking for properties, and they're not finding the ones that I was finding. So, the houses are out there, they're just not being able to be connected. And so, part of what I want to kind of pivot my role to be is to help educate landlords on how to get these opportunities, where to get these opportunities, how to work with the relocation companies, so that everybody wins. You know, the relocation company gets something, they get to house their employee or the family that's been displaced. And then the real estate investor, my fellow real estate investor, gets to get a nice juicy lease, and you know, maybe a 6-month booking. And I love that. I love being in that win-win position. And so, I really want to help, especially long-term landlords, understand that this is an option, even if they have an unfurnished property, they could be able to get bookings. And there's really no huge upfront investment to even get started. If they have availability, it's possible that they could get these opportunities, too. And, you know, maybe fill in a small gap, or maybe even just keep going with mid-term. Now, Abby, are you seeing any markets right now that stand out to you that have just a high amount of demand and just not enough supply where maybe these are markets to go into to start investing. It's a good question. Um I would say that there's opportunity all over the place. You know, it doesn't have to be big cities. It can actually sometimes be more advantageous in those smaller rural areas, you know, maybe an hour outside of the city, you know, because that's where there's really limited availability. So, being able to have a rental property that's flexible is would really give you an advantage. Yeah, that's a great point as like having a property that you're able to kind of combine strategies. And I used to do Airbnb arbitrage. I had some apartments in a complex and that's basically what we had done there was we would do mid-term rental and it was, you know, just trying to find a traveling nurse that was at the hospital nearby to stay in there when, you know, we had no bookings for a while, we'd turn it on to Airbnb, switch that flip on, and rent it short-term on there. So, especially if you have an existing property with an existing strategy is trying out a mid-term rental and then being able to pivot there. Yeah, for sure. Abby, I've seen that in your platform you also have like a strong AI in the foundation when you built this. So, how is AI going to change the way that you see landlords operating and how did you build this into your platform specifically? So, we have um you know, a couple of AI components built in and I think that AI is only going to become more essential in in what we're doing. Again, you know, the way the world is going, I think it's impossible to avoid. And if we're not using it, then it's, you know, we we're going to be left behind. And so, no matter what you think about AI, I think that it's important because there's functionalities here that can help us. And I'll continue to keep learning on how we can improve the functionality of the site for both sides. And if there's something that we can do using AI, I'm I'm definitely going to try and do that. And like I said, this was really built initially for relocation companies to use as a as a resource, as a tool. But that also means that it's a really good place for landlords. And so my hope is that as we continue to work with relocation companies and understand how this platform can be more beneficial to them, we can then also integrate how it's more beneficial for landlords. And like I said, being on both sides of this transaction myself, I really understand what the relocation companies need, but also what landlords want and how we can how I can help both sides to come together and everyone gets a win-win. Now, having that experience being on both sides of it, has your mindset shifted at all going from just the investor with a mid-term rental to now seeing both sides of it? Yeah, I mean, I think understanding how truly how these relocation companies work was a big eye-opener. Um also working with insurance displacements it was a real eye-opener for me because I I think I never really considered what happens when somebody has damage to their home. You know, and and thankfully I've never had to be in that situation before. And and so I think if you haven't experienced it or know somebody that's experienced it, you you don't really think about where the people stay while that happens. And the reality is that these people are going through potentially some of the worst things they've ever experienced. And that that's serious. I mean, it's real life things happening. And when you start connecting with the families that are going through these awful situations, so often they're just so humble. They're just so grateful for the help and having somewhere safe and comfortable. And that kind of became our priority also when we when I started doing the business a few years ago was I want to find somewhere safe and comfortable for this family to stay. And so that was a bit of a driving force to me to find somebody in my community that had a property that fit what they needed because then we could find somewhere for this family to stay that was safe and comfortable. And so, yeah, certainly understanding that it's it's shaped me a lot and and certainly the way that we run the business. Now, on the insurance side of things, I can imagine that, you know, especially in these situations where something tragic happens to their home and it's not livable, these are pretty quick renters. Like you're getting them in within days. So, this is this a pretty quick process then from the day they're making their claim till the the day they're moving into your property? Yeah. Yeah, it's it's a very fast process and um typically the family is already in a hotel. And so, the sooner that we can get them into the home the better. It can go as quick as same day sometimes, but often it takes a few days, you know, to go through the process of getting insurance adjuster approval and, you know, do lease agreements, background checks, you know, whatever it is that we need to do. Yeah, typically it's it's a few days. If it's an unfurnished property, then there's the process of just organizing the furniture, which typically the insurance will do through a furniture rental company. But, yeah, a few days typically. But, again, that's important for the landlord, you know, if they have that immediate availability. That's something also that you can factor in with with pricing. If you're going to stay available, typically for me, I don't take bookings in the future. So, I will have my current tenant. I typically do a 30-day notice to make a and so, once we get towards the end of that, I'll check in with them, "Hey, do you need to extend?" If it's a no, then I'll start to advertise again, but I don't take future bookings just in case because I could get an insurance claim that might be 6 months, 9 months, maybe even longer and I want to be available for those. And that that's so interesting to me is so how that process works. And I guess my last question on that piece is do you know how long they're staying or you have no idea when you first get them in or an idea of it? So typically the insurance will ask for a certain length lease up front, but honestly I would say about 90% of our contracts do get extended even if it's just by one more month. >> Yeah. The insurance generally tends to air on the side of caution in terms of lease length because they don't want to over promise and then end up having to pay to break a lease. So they might ask for 3 months or 6 months up front and then continue month to month after that just in case the repairs aren't complete. And there's so many factors when they're repairing a home, you know, I'm sure if you're dealing with this with your house. It's you know, between repairs and materials and contractors and permits and there's so many things to factor in and and delays happen. And so keeping that open availability is really important especially for insurance claims. Okay, well I actually do have one more follow up on that piece. So you're actually writing the lease agreement with the insurance company and they're responsible for paying. Are they also providing a security deposit and what happens if the tenants damage the property? Is the insurance company now on the hook for recovering you know, paying for those damages? Yeah, it's a good question. So typically the insurance relocation companies are not the ones that are on the lease. So the lease is actually between the tenant and the landlord. And so through what the way we work through ARROS is that the landlord can take a security deposit of whatever amount that they feel comfortable with, you know, whatever their the security deposit normally is, which is something else that kind of differentiates us from some of the other platforms that are out there, which you know, just gives you a little bit more protection. And you know, I encourage landlords to still do their due diligence even if it's an insurance claim, even if it's a company that's coming in. You know, we give you the opportunity to be able to take the information and do a background check. You know, because ultimately, the way that it works with insurance is it is between the tenant and the landlord. And so, it would work the same as any other rental in terms of if there's damage, that would come out of the security deposit or ultimately if it was really bad, I guess, you know, be insurance, home insurance or the renter's insurance or whichever you would fall back on. But, that would function the same as any other any other tenancy. Well, Abby, before we wrap up here, uh for any landlord that's listening right now and they want to get started with their first mid-term rental placement or, you know, maybe even somebody that wants their first relocation company client, what are some of the steps that they should take this week, the action items you would assign them? Yeah, so I think, you know, they're welcome to sign up to Arise. So, you can sign up at www.stayarise.com. We're still working all over the country, but we are kind of prioritizing Texas and Ohio. So, if there is rental properties there, that you're more likely to see more volume coming through in those areas. I think that having things ready, your pricing, your fee structure, if you accept pets, how much do you charge, what your cleaning fee is, having all of those things ready to go so that when somebody does come and asks you, you are ready with the information, ready to respond. If you get a call or an inquiry, respond as soon as possible. Hopefully within a couple of hours. Um because it could be that they find something else and move on just like that. So, if you wait too long, you might miss the opportunity. So, speed is definitely of the essence. Well, Abby, thank you so much for joining me today on Be a Better Landlord. Um and thank you for sharing your platform and your experience and your journey um with mid-term rentals. Yeah, thank Thank having me. And just as a little thank you, if anybody wants to reach out and find me on Instagram, you can find me at the Abby Horton. And if you want to give me a follow and a DM with the word Ashley, then I'll send my managing MTR out of state top tips. Oh, thank you so much for sharing that with us. Of course, my pleasure. Well, thank you guys so much for listening to Be a Better Landlord, and I can't wait to see you guys next time.

metadata.author: Jorge Garcia | Roadmap Lodging
metadata.shortDescription:
Corporate housing inquiries: 1-855-552-9155 What if your house burned down tonight…
Where would your family live, and who would pay for it?

In this video, I break down how insurance relocation REALLY works and why insurance companies are willing (and required) to pay $5,000–$12,000+ per month for fully furnished homes.

Most rental hosts think insurance housing is rare or complicated.
It’s not.

Insurance relocation starts with a crisis, a fire, flood, storm, or major damage, and that triggers something called Additional Living Expenses (ALE) inside the homeowner’s insurance policy.

That ALE coverage is what funds long-term, fully furnished housing while a home is being repaired.

And here’s the key most hosts miss 👇
This isn’t short-term rental.
This is midterm rental with pre-approved budgets, longer stays, and predictable income.

In this video, you’ll learn:

Why insurance companies prefer homes over hotels

What ALE coverage actually pays for (it’s more than rent)

How long insurance placements REALLY last (60–180+ days)

Why insurance relocation pays more than traditional rentals

How the same house can earn 2–3X just by changing the client

Why experienced operators love insurance guests

You’re not renting a house.
You’re stabilizing a family during one of the worst moments of their life, and solving a massive claims problem for insurance companies.

That’s why the budgets exist.

If you’re tired of nightly pricing, constant turnovers, and unpredictable income, insurance relocation might be the cleanest path into high-paying midterm rentals.

If you want me to break down exactly how hosts get approved with insurance housing companies and adjusters, comment “SHOW ME”.

metadata.author: Jesse Vasquez
metadata.shortDescription:
You can make THOUSANDS more a month on your mid-term rentals by NOT renting to traveling nurses and renting with insurance companies instead. About every eighty-eight seconds, a house fire occurs somewhere in the US. This displaces families who now need a safe place to stay while their homes get rebuilt/repaired. And that's where you come in.

Relocation managers like Serge Kozhukhar work with mid-term rental operators (including me!) to move disaster-struck families from hotels into temporary homes. And here's the thing: you can make THOUSANDS more a month using this strategy while helping those who need a home away from home. 

How much do insurance companies pay? Which houses make the cut? What do relocation managers look for in mid-term rentals? metadata.title: Understanding Additional Living Expense Coverage in Homeowners Insurance
metadata.author: Insurance Savvy
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, we break down what Additional Living Expense (ALE) coverage is and how it can help you in times of need. When a covered peril makes your home uninhabitable, ALE can cover costs like temporary housing, meals, and other essential living expenses. We’ll explain how ALE works, what it typically covers, and why it's crucial for homeowners to understand this aspect of their insurance policy. Don’t get caught off guard—watch now to learn how to protect yourself and your family!

metadata.title: What is Loss of Use Coverage on your Homeowner's Insurance?
metadata.author: Crowley Insurance Agency, Inc
metadata.shortDescription:
Loss of use is the coverage to help you pay for living expenses if you need to live somewhere else temporarily because your primary home is uninhabitable due to a claim.

The coverage can help with extra costs associated with staying in a hotel, doing laundry at a laundromat, or going out to eat at a restaurant. For larger claims with a longer repair time, the insurance may look to rent an apartment or house while your home is being repaired or rebuilt.
_

For more information on how you can save money on your insurance give us a call (315) 437-2983 or visit us https://www.crowleyinsurance.com/ 

202 N Center St, East Syracuse, NY 13057

metadata.title: Increasing Your Rental Income 3 to 4 Times by Providing Corporate Housing with Angela Healy
metadata.author: RPOAM Real Estate Investor Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
#corporatehousing #longtermrentals #realestateinvesting

Rental Property Owner & Real Estate Investor Podcast | RPOA (Rental Property Owners Association) | https://rpoaonline.org

Episode 364

If you’ve been listening long enough to this show, then you’re already familiar with the concept of corporate and executive rental housing, in which the property owner provides furnished 30 day or longer stays to families and business travelers.

My guest today has taken corporate housing a step further and franchised the concept.

Angela Healy is the CEO and co-owner of AvenueWest, a national corporate housing provider, which was recently ranked as the 15th fastest growing real estate company in America by Inc. Magazine.

Today Angela defines what corporate housing is, the demand, and the profit potential from this lucrative niche. We’ll also go into detail on the franchise model, and how that can allow individual property owners get into this space.

You can find out more about Angela:
angela@avenuewest.com

Today’s episode is brought to you by Green Property Management, managing everything from single family homes to apartment complexes in the West Michigan area.

https://www.livegreenlocal.com/

And RCB & Associates, helping Michigan-based real estate investors and small business owners navigate the complex world of health insurance and Medicare benefits.

https://www.rcbassociatesllc.com/

If you're new here, I'm Aurelio Licata, founder of Arbitrage Empire. My team and I help everyday people start and scale a profitable Airbnb business through rental arbitrage: you lease the property, list it on Airbnb, and run it as a short-term rental without ever buying real estate. We've built a seven-figure Airbnb portfolio across 50+ U.S. markets, and we use that exact playbook to place clients in proven markets so they're not guessing where to start.

A few years ago my life looked nothing like this. I was a Division 1 baseball player chasing the pros until three surgeries ended that dream and left me with a few thousand dollars and no plan. I found Airbnb arbitrage, paid a mentor with basically my last few cents, and put my head down for 18 months. That one decision changed everything.

My takeaways:

1. Take the leap even when it's scary. You don't need to feel ready, you just need to start.

2. Surround yourself with the right people. If everyone around you works a 9 to 5 and never questions it, that becomes your ceiling too.

3. Never be afraid to pivot. Adversity usually isn't the end of the road, it's just redirecting you to where you're supposed to be.

If you've ever thought about starting an Airbnb business, bet on yourself and go after it. Your life can look completely different a year from now

In this episode of The Mid-Term Rental Movement, host Vivian Yip sits down with Gabriel Wacker, Vice President of Sales & Marketing at Viciniti, to pull back the curtain on the corporate housing industry—the original blueprint behind today’s mid-term rental model.

Gabriel shares how corporate housing has quietly operated since the 1980s, why 95% occupancy rates are possible without relying on Airbnb, and how dynamic inventory strategies like match leasing, arbitrage, and B2B partnerships create long-term stability.

You’ll learn what truly separates professional corporate housing operators from casual mid-term rentals, why relationships—not listings—drive demand, and how single-family homes are reshaping the future of furnished rentals. This episode also explores relocation trends, flex housing budgets, insurance displacement stays, and why many corporations restrict Airbnb usage altogether.

If you’re a mid-term rental operator, real estate investor, or host looking to scale beyond platforms and build predictable, professional income, this conversation will completely change how you see the furnished rental ecosystem.

And that's what I think is a little bit different. I mean, I think mid-term rental operators could do this if they wanted to kind of expand the portfolio. We do a lot of setting up units, tearing down units based on demand. So, if a somebody has a large intern group, 50 to 100 units that they need, we'll go get that inventory. It's not sitting in our inventory right now. We'll go build that inventory just for that, whatever it is, two or two or three months. We'll create inventory just for that. So, there's a dynamic inventory is what I like to use the phrase is we're, you know, what's great about corporate housing just in general in the corporate housing world, there's a lot of great operators out there that we can build housing based on what the customer needs. We can build customized housing solutions. >> Yeah, that's I think that's really that's really um that's awesome. Number one because when we, at least as a supply chain practitioner and professional, we're always talking about business agility and being able to adapt to certain situations, like the breaking up and tearing down and being flexible, cuz we know projects cancel, we know projects extend. You know, I'm I'm it sounds like you guys have really have a formula for supporting those those dynamic businesses. >> Yeah, it does help. So, we like you said, we have a furniture rental company called Furniture Options. So, we have 12 warehouses throughout the Midwest down through Texas where we have furniture, housewares, everything in large warehouses. So, we can easily set up a unit pretty quickly. But, if somebody wanted to get in that space, they can rent from either Furniture Options or another. I know you spoke with Court Furniture recently. There's furniture rental providers out there that can do this for you to make those where you can build those those units or build the inventory up when you have the clients that need them. >> Funny, I was just looking through my stack of cards yesterday and I came up to Furniture Options and I didn't realize that was your furniture division. >> Yep. Yep, same company. >> Amazing. And you guys have national coverage or >> Really just in the Midwest for Furniture Options. So, Furniture Options, we are in kind of an eight-state region right in the middle of the country, kind of Iowa and Oma- or Iowa and Nebraska down to Texas and Louisiana, kind of that strip right there is where we what we service. >> Got it. So, I'm curious, you came to our MTR Summit event pre-event, which was the School of Hard Knocks Midterm Rental Edition. I was actually really excited to see your name pop up cuz we'd met a few times at the CHPA conference. And when I saw your name pop up, I was like, "Hmm, I wonder if the the corporate housing people are interested in what's happening in the midterm rental space." I'm curious, what um what do you see happening from your perspective with the growth and interest of midterm rentals as a real estate strategy? >> Yeah, I think there's definitely interest in, you know, I think the CHPA world is what's what's going on over in the midterm rental space. And I think I have interest too. From we have a furniture rental company, so I feel like there's opportunities there for our furniture division. Um but, I also want to make sure that there's I've met some great operators in the midterm rental space. I think they're doing a great job. But, I also want to make sure that there's not bad operators out there that are using the term corporate housing cuz I don't want the corporate housing term to get used loosely cuz we traditionally try to set ourselves apart as a profession. We are very professional. Most of the operators within CHBA Um and that was another interest that I had. I also sit on the membership committee. I am one of the chairs for the membership committee for CHBA. So, looking for opportunities to add members to our CHBA uh community. >> What um what benefit do you think someone would have by joining CHBA, especially if they maybe only have one or two properties or versus someone that has multiple? >> Yeah, I think twofold. I think education, I think there's a lot of association for CHBA is made up of small companies. 80, I think 84% of the member companies are small businesses, small companies. So, I think you There's a lot of members there that you could talk to that you could learn best practices, housekeeping strategies, operations. There's a lot of learning that can happen at CHBA. And then also, like I said earlier, there's a lot of renting between corporate housing companies. So, that's another way that you can you can build up inventory, but you can mitigate some of your risk by renting some units from other operators and then just marking up a little bit. So, you can get to that 50 or 100 units that you need to have for that client. So, or your We don't set up our own inventory outside of kind of like that territory that I was talking about. We typically work with partners in the corporate housing world for East Coast, West Coast, and then we'll mark it up a little bit and offer that to our client. That's the model that we work with. So, we've made those relationships with those those partners that we work with and that's why I think becoming a member of CHBA can be valuable is you can make those relationship, get business out of it, but also learn um some good strategies on how to run your business. >> Yeah, I I've certainly learned a lot. I participate in the free info sessions that they have about pricing and revenue and and things like that. Plus, participating in both of the CHPA conferences for the last 2 years, partly because our our was nominated for the Innovation Award for Tower of Excellence. So, that was that was really awesome. One I mean, you you talked a few times about becoming a like being a professional corporate housing company. What what does it mean to be a professional corporate housing? Like what if someone wanted to level up, right? From the mid-term rental space. What makes a corporate housing company different? Like what do you what does professionalism mean? >> Typically, it's on the operation side. So, we're looking at standard furniture, standard housewares. And sometimes that might end up looking a little cookie-cutter, but like we make sure there's consistency across our brand. I can't necessarily speak for all the members within CHBA, but what we try to do is we standardize all of our practices. So, whether it's the furnishings and the housewares, they all look some the same number of pieces, furniture pieces, and houseware items are in all of our apartments. And then just the inspection process that most of CHBA members go through what we go through is pretty intense. So, there's a checklist, you take photos, you take videos, you make sure that everything is in working condition, everything's clean and ready for the guests when they arrive. I think those are the things that you see as the standard standardizing practices, inventory, and operations is what constitute a professional service is what I would say. >> Yeah, I agree with that. That's why whenever our company moves a client in, we are sending a third-party inspector. It's not we're not trying to bust people for doing a bad job or anything like that. We're just trying to maintain a standard and protect our our reputation and relationships. So, you know, at the end of the day, if we're working with corporate housing people or even with insurance displaced families, they're going through something that they probably don't love going through, you know, having to move your house and move into somewhere strange. And being able to provide a professional level of service that says, "Hey, we've gone through and made sure that the washer and dryer works, that the locks that there's not going to be an issue arriving when they show up at 2:00 in the morning, and that all the light bulbs are are working, and that there's no dust on the fan." Things like that. I think those are really like good touches to put in your operations business to provide that level of service. >> Yeah, and I think, you know, we we typically So, we have an app that we send to when we're working with a partner, we send that to them to that, so they will take It's a checklist, but they also take photos and videos showing us so we can visit visually see everything's in working condition. And it's as, you know, some of the things might seem silly, but it's like turning on every burner on the stove and showing that they're they're they're turning on, showing that the microwave is actually working, making sure there's not lint in the in the dryer. You know, those things, looking under the bed. Uh those are the things that we expect from our partners when we work with them. >> You know, one thing that I think people overlook is hot water. >> Yeah. >> As you I mean, sometimes when you're doing these on-demand leasing, or even if you're setting up a brand new mid-term rental, you may have thought you turned on all the utilities, and then you're like, "Oh my gosh, I forgot this one thing." So, these are, you know, the inspection process is really to help everyone real >> Yeah. >> make sure that they're on the same page to providing that great experience. >> Yeah, I know that's one of the first things when I go and when I do an inspection, I'll turn the hot water on. Usually, I kind of like high items, I'll start with hot water, internet, you know, those are the things. Go to the breaker box, make sure there's nothing flipped on the breaker box. Like those things you start with, and you kind of move backwards from like low high highest level of importance to Internet's going to be one of the first things you have to check because that's critical for our for our guests that stay with us. Um I think we see companies try it then not try it and go back and forth. So, I don't wouldn't say that's new. It's definitely not new. It's been around like flex or flex has been around a long time. Lump sum's been around a lot long time. We have heard of more companies going to kind of a cafeteria plan. What and what I mean by that is they usually is a point system. So, you can get you'll get a certain amount of points and you can use it either for your home sale or your home purchase, temp housing expense or like so you can kind of pick and choose what you use based on um and So, I don't think that's new, but it's I think people companies are definitely looking for cost savings. I think that's what we see more than a change in in policy. It's more just companies are looking for savings whether that's temp housing or just relocations in general. Relocations are down for the last two or three years. Um there's a lot of reasons for that, but I think we've seen relocations um have changed a lot in the last several years. >> I remember seeing the bill both times when I relocated once with Tetra Pak back in 2005 and then I relocated again with Apple under a relocation package. That was in 2014 and I was astonished at how expensive corporate housing was. Have you heard something like that at all? >> They Yes. Yeah, there's going to be policies in place from either the relocation management company or the end user client whether what kind of inventory that they want supplied to their guests. Because they want to make sure that the service is going to be excellent, like what we talked about previously. It's just not a big piece right now. >> Now we don't have anything listed on Airbnb, but we've used it here and there in the past to fill fill some vacancies. >> Got it. So, it's our inventory strategy and then the relationships that we've built. So, we're you know, getting continuous business to keep them full. So, kind of using those different strategies to maximize our our occupancy is it's a day-to-day thing. Like, it's always something that we talk about. We talk about occupancy on a daily basis. >> Got it. So, do you do you think midterm rentals is a threat at all do you guys? Like, if you guys were to do a SWOT analysis today at Vicinity, does the the Airbnb host come up in in one of the quadrants? >> I think midterm rental operators, for sure. I think there's some really good operators out there that can be a a threat. I mean, Airbnb has been around for 20 years now. I I it's so it's not that part's not new. I think the professionalization of some of the midterm rental operators can be a threat to corporate housing operators. Um so, that for sure. I I think their model's a little bit different. Um so, sometimes we're seeing those in more often in single-family homes versus apartment communities, so there's it's a little bit not apples to apples, but for sure, I think there's some good operators out there. >> Are you seeing any change cuz I I I know a lot of the midterm rental operators at at least in my community, a lot of them are hosting single-family homes or have a collection of single-family homes. Uh so, yeah, we've seen more and more of the single-family home in the last 10 years. >> I see. Okay, well, that's that's really good to know um cuz I deal in mostly the single family home space. So I'm always curious to know if you see what's trending. Another question I I guess I wanted to ask. You guys work with a lot of the insurance relocation companies. Is that correct? >> Yeah. >> Are you seeing a stronger trend towards unfurnished requests? >> It's a complex question. I mean that so we we have a furniture rental company that works with all the insurance housing companies also. So we've they've always had that model. They've always had a model where they're looking for unfurnished homes and then they set up the the furniture and the housewares and do that models traditionally the model that they've done. Um we're putting together pricing, SLAs, like we're all that's happening right now. So it's anywhere from we have you know, some that need it right away and some that are looking out at next year already. Traditionally, like we look at a you know, it's we don't see a lot of bookings more than a month or two out. We We don't take a lot of We don't do short-term bookings. We We're going to tell the client, yes, we will procure this inventory for you. We'll make sure this happens, but we won't lock up our current inventory for something much more than a month out at a time. >> Got it. Well, that's good good indication to know. metadata.title: No Property? No Problem: How to Master Rental Arbitrage
metadata.author: Adam James Speaks
metadata.shortDescription:
Why would a landlord stop renting to anyone else and hand every property to one person? Adam James tells the story, and explains how to start an Airbnb business without owning a single property (rental arbitrage).

Stay for these moments:
- Why a house that wouldn't sell in December became one of the first Airbnbs in Tulsa
- What happened when his very first guests came to adopt a child
- What a landlord did when she saw the Airbnb price, and how Adam answered
- Why he hasn't been to one of his own houses in years
- Why getting choked out in jiu-jitsu is the best business training he knows

Chapters:
00:00 Opening prayer
02:14 Adam and his two companies
03:42 How many doors does he run?
05:27 How Adam got into Airbnb
11:06 Making money on other people's property
15:32 What is rental arbitrage?
27:46 The biggest aha moments
28:28 The roof popper story
32:34 Midterm rentals and insurance placements
35:48 Landlords and the Zillow price
39:47 Running it on systems
44:22 Work hard to be lazy: automation
47:10 The same software from 5 doors to 200
49:39 Three businesses that work together
52:44 Faith
55:31 Why Adam does jiu-jitsu
56:38 Close

Which part hit you hardest? What's the one thing stopping you from starting? Tell me in the comments.

New eyes. New business. New freedom.
adamjamesspeaks.com

metadata.title: Mid-Term Rentals 101 (2025): Watch This FIRST — Leases, Deposits & Listings
metadata.author: Jesse Vasquez
metadata.shortDescription:
-Mid-Term Rentals 101 (2025). Watch this first.
In this live Midterm Monday, I break down the simple setup that actually works: the lease you need, how to handle security deposits, and the best places to list so you can go from empty to booked fast. No gimmicks. Just the foundations that scale.

What you’ll learn:

- The exact lease structure I use for 30, 60, 90 days and why I roll to month-to-month
- How I decide deposit amounts for individuals vs corporate clients
- House rules that prevent headaches later
- Where to list for 30+ day stays and how to be proactive beyond platforms
- Monthly check-ins, pet policies, cleaning cadence, and move-in checklists
- Simple gear and furnishings that survive real-world use

Resources mentioned
• Free templates and guides: mtrstrategy.com
• Starter Pack training: https://www.airventureacademy.com/starter-pack
• My podcast, The JV Pod: https://open.spotify.com/show/1WLQAJuNjHtT3cQBHpyaUB?si=1cb37d2e871f4517
• TurboTenant for leases and payments: https://shorturl.at/DPEBr

About me
I’m Jesse Vasquez. I help operators land high-paying mid-term rental contracts and build a real business around 30+ day stays. I go live every Monday at 4pm PT.

Legal note
I am not an attorney. This video is for education only. Check your local and state laws and talk to your attorney before using any lease language or policies.

metadata.shortDescription:
When the constant cycle of cleanings, check-ins, and shifting local ordinances starts feeling like a second full-time job, nightly hosting can wear you down fast.

But you don’t have to choose between burning out or locking into an inflexible 12-month lease. There’s a middle path that many independent hosts choose: the mid-term rental.

In this video, we break down:
- How mid-term rentals compare to short- and long-term models
- Why this setup fits residential neighborhoods
- Who your ideal guests are and where to find them
- The core questions to ask before deciding if it fits you and your home

Want the free guide that answers the question, “Why Pivot to a Different Type of Rental”? Comment MIDTERM below and we’ll send the link directly to your inbox.

metadata.shortDescription:
Ready to buy your first boutique hotel? Apply for the hotel mastermind and we'll help you find it, underwrite it, manage it, or partner on it with you.

Apply here: https://boutiquehotelsecrets.com/#bhs-apply

Get $20 off per listing at Furnished Finder: *STR20*

Airbnb now takes 15.5% from hosts. Furnished Finder charges $199 a year. Jeff Hurst, former President of Vrbo and former COO of Expedia Group, explains why midterm rentals are growing faster than short term rentals, and how hosts can make the switch.

Jeff is the President and CEO of Furnished Finder, the largest furnished monthly rental marketplace in the U.S. He has competed with Airbnb since 2010, including as Chief Strategy Officer at HomeAway and President of Vrbo.

In this episode of the STR Secrets Podcast, Mike Sjogren and Mike Reilly ask Jeff how midterm rentals compare to long term and short term rentals, what to do if your STR market got regulated, and whether AI booking will replace Airbnb and Vrbo.

*TIMESTAMPS*
0:00 Intro
0:32 What Furnished Finder is and how it works
2:50 Jeff's background at HomeAway, Vrbo, and Expedia
3:19 Why midterm rental demand is up over 30%
5:39 Are small multifamily owners converting to midterm?
6:29 How to underwrite a midterm rental
8:21 Room rentals and co living
9:30 New Furnished Finder features and Market Insights
12:27 Syncing calendars for a hybrid STR and midterm strategy
14:34 Why you need to block 60 to 120 days on Airbnb
15:22 Airbnb's 15.5% host fee vs a $199 subscription
18:21 Bulk pricing for property managers
20:03 What to do if your STR market got regulated
23:18 Will AI and agentic booking replace the OTAs?
28:45 Yard signs and the Extended Stay America trick
29:24 The best markets for midterm rentals
31:32 Where midterm rentals are heading in the next 5 years
37:01 Must haves for new midterm rental investors
40:15 Where to learn more about Furnished Finder
42:05 Jeff's number one secret to success

*KEY QUESTIONS ANSWERED*
What is a midterm rental?
A midterm rental is a furnished rental for stays of 30 days or longer. On Furnished Finder, the average stay is about 100 days, and tenants are mostly traveling nurses, corporate workers, relocating families, and grad students.

How much more can a midterm rental make than a long term rental?
Jeff says furniture usually pays for itself in 6 to 12 months. After that, a well run midterm rental can earn 30 to 50% more rent than a 12 month lease, with occupancy in the mid 90s in the right area.

How should you underwrite a midterm rental?
Jeff's rule: your worst case is your long term rent. Underwrite at market rent for a 12 month lease, then factor in furnishing costs, occupancy, and pricing.

How much does it cost to furnish a midterm rental?
Jeff says it typically costs about $7 per square foot to furnish a midterm rental, compared to $45 to $50 per square foot for a high performing short term rental in a competitive market.

How much does Furnished Finder cost?
Furnished Finder is a $199 per year subscription with no booking commission. Jeff says that works out to about a 1 to 2% take rate for a high performing listing. Property managers with 5 or more listings can get bulk pricing at partnerships@furnishedfinder.com.

Where is midterm rental demand strongest?
Near hospitals, good school districts, commuter corridors, and construction. Abilene, Texas has been one of Furnished Finder's fastest growing markets because of new data center construction.

Will AI replace Airbnb and Vrbo?
Jeff doesn't think so. He expects AI to change how guests discover properties, but believes the big OTAs will still win most bookings. He sees maybe 5 to 10% of bookings shifting to new direct sources.

What should you do if your STR market got regulated?
Jeff says continuing to run it as a short term rental is probably the worst option, and selling might be the second worst. Converting to a midterm rental is often the best path forward.

*RESOURCES MENTIONED*
Furnished Finder: https://www.furnishedfinder.com
Landlord Diaries Podcast: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/landlord-diaries-the-monthly-rentals-podcast/id1641540804
Property manager partnerships: partnerships@furnishedfinder.com

*ABOUT JEFF HURST*
Jeff Hurst is President and CEO of Furnished Finder. He joined in late 2023 after two decades in online travel as COO of Expedia Group, President of Vrbo, and Chief Strategy Officer at HomeAway. He holds an MBA from Stanford Graduate School of Business and started his career at McKinsey & Company.

*ABOUT STR SECRETS*
STR Secrets helps short term rental owners and property managers build profitable, systemized businesses that buy back their time. Hosted by Mike Sjogren and Mike Reilly.
Subscribe for weekly episodes on short term rentals, midterm rentals, property management, and real estate investing.

A single mid-term rental can stay booked year-round with just 2 to 4 travel nurse tenants. In this episode of The Landlord Diaries, co-hosts Kelly Bailey and Katie Lyon break down how to attract healthcare professionals on Furnished Finder, how to price against Airbnb, which amenities actually matter, and the top cities being searched by healthcare professionals right now.

Travel nurses are one of the most reliable tenant types in the mid-term rental space. Their contracts run 13 weeks on average and many extend an extra term. If you are a real estate investor, landlord, retiree exploring a side hustle, long-term rental owner looking for stronger cashflow, or short-term rental host navigating new regulations, this episode walks you through the full playbook.


What you'll learn:
- How Airbnb's 15.5% fee structure compares to Furnished Finder's flat annual price
- How renting by the room turned a $2,200/mo booking into $2,500/mo
- Why travel nursing is not in decline, despite the rumors
- How Market Insights helps you find out if your area has healthcare demand
- The 3 protection layers every mid-term rental landlord needs: tenant screening, lease, damage protection plan
- The top 10 cities being searched by healthcare professionals in the last 30 days

Questions we will answer:
- How can property owners effectively market to travel nurses and agencies?
- Which platforms specialize in matching travel nurses with temporary housing?
- What search terms and amenities are most important for healthcare professionals?
- How do landlords safely rent furnished properties to travel nurses?

With 300,000 monthly rental listings across all 50 states, Furnished Finder is the leading platform for travel nurse housing, business travelers, academics, and families relocating. Whether you own one ADU or a growing portfolio, this episode gives you the systems to turn mid-term rentals into reliable, high-occupancy income.

metadata.title: Watch this Before Renting on Furnished Finder
metadata.author: Midterm Rental Consulting
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, I answer the most common questions new and experienced landlords ask when setting up a midterm rental on Furnished Finder.

You’ll learn:

📍 The safest way to handle a rental security deposit (and why most landlords get this wrong)
📍 How to avoid legal trouble with deposit misuse and stay compliant with state laws
📍 Why I don’t recommend using Furnished Finder’s damage protection program
📍 Whether allowing pets is worth the risk—and how it can increase demand and occupancy
📍 Simple ways to make your rental more attractive to pet owners (especially dog owners)
📍 How to set seasonal pricing tiers (low, mid, high) to avoid vacancies and maximize income
📍 What actually matters to renters (and why your mortgage doesn’t)

➕Work with me: https://stan.store/erin_spradlin
➕Free Rental Resources: https://stan.store/erin_spradlin
➕ Furnished Rental Must-Haves Checklist: https://erinspradlin.substack.com/
➕ Midterm Rental Books on Amazon: https://amzn.to/47psD1s

If you’re asking:
📍 “Why isn’t my Furnished Finder listing getting booked?”
📍 “Should I allow dogs in my rental?”
📍 “How do I avoid losing money as a landlord?”

—this video walks you through practical, real-world strategies to set up your rental correctly from the start.

Perfect for landlords who want a more passive, low-maintenance rental that stays occupied and profitable.

#MonthlyRentals, #DigitalNomad, #AirbnbMonthly, #LongTermStay, #CozyListing, #RemoteWork, and #Staycation

Thanks for watching and supporting my channel, as always please give a like and subscribe, it really helps me grow on this platform which is one of my big goals!

Looking for a lucrative side hustle that fits into your busy life? In this episode of the Furnished Finder Landlord Diaries podcast, hosts Kelly Bailey & Katie Lyon dive into how Lara secured 100% of her bookings through Furnished Finder, partnered with an upscale apartment complex, and self-manages her out-of-state rentals with ease.

List Your Property Now on Furnished Finder:

segments.text: Talking to a landlord in order to run their property on Airbnb can be a very touchy
conversation if you don't know how to approach it in today's video I'm going to be talking about how
I overcome objections in order to create win-win situations with landlords so that
they can say yes to me renting their property and getting permission in writing before I do
make sure you guys subscribe to my channel and turn on the notification bell hey everyone my
name is Jorge Contreras and I am on track to do over 2 million dollars of Airbnb Revenue in 2022 and most
of that revenue is actually from the subleasing strategy by renting properties getting permission
in writing and launching them on Airbnb I learned that this specific strategy no down payments no
closing costs has allowed me to really accelerate my cash flow by the way have you tried speaking to
landlords and maybe it didn't work out as planned or maybe you did and there's something that worked
for you please let me know in the comment down below so let's go over the five biggest objections
that are most common when speaking to property owners and here it is it's that they want to be
paid on time and I totally get it these investors are in the business for mailbox money they want
their safe and secure fixed amount of money every single month and often when they hear that we are
going to be running a business and that our revenues will actually fluctuate they might
misinterpret that and feel that what they're going to receive from you is also going to fluctuate so
you want to clarify that what they're going to be getting paid every single month is the exact
amount that they were advertising on Zelo or wherever you found the property so typically
part of how I overcome this objection is that I'm going to set up the property on autopay
and on top of that I'm going to set it up two days early so that they get their money on time
every single month and they never have to worry about getting a late fee or the payment changing
and then of course in the lease agreement we are going to have the terms right how much I'm paying
every month for the duration of the 12 months so it definitely gives them peace of mind that
everything is going to be in writing the second objection is they want their property to be taken
care of they realize that people will be checking in checking out you're going to have you know four
to eight guests per month on Airbnb and so their concern is hey what about repairs what if there's
any you know wear and tear or just things that are directly caused by your guest so the way I
overcome that objection is I tell the landlord Hey listen any repairs or damages that are directly
caused by my guest I will be 100 responsible and we can put it in writing now obviously if
the repairs or the damages or wear and tear has nothing to do with my guest and more with the
wear and tear of their property then that's going to be the responsibility of the owner let me give
you an example imagine there's an AC system that's been there for 10 years and it goes out well that
was not caused by my guests right so the owner is going to be responsible for that but if there's
a hole in the wall or maybe they cause the leak and one of the bathroom showers anything that is
directly caused by my guest I will be responsible and then what I'm going to do is I'm going to
charge the guest just like when you stay at a hotel the hotel is going to ask for your credit
card for incidentals and if you create any type of damage guess what they will charge your card
on file well Airbnb works the exact same way if there's any type of damage we can submit a claim
and then collect the fees and we have the ability to charge their credit card up until 14 days after
their checkout the third objection that comes up often is hey Jorge what about the neighbors
you know we've been living here for you know 12 years we're not moving to a different location
and we want to make sure that you maintain a great relationship with the neighbors we don't
want to upset anybody so the way I answer to that is hey landlord don't worry I totally understand
how you feel I would want to make sure that I have a good relationship with the Airbnb next door if I
was living next door as well so typically what we do landlord is I will go and personally introduce
myself to the neighbors to the right to the left across and behind me since they are the ones who
will like likely see guests coming in and out I'm going to give them my business card let them know
that we're going to be running a short-term rental business however we are going to be running a very
tight shift and if they ever see or hear anything they can go ahead and contact me directly if you
guys are ready to make 2022 your year and finally launch your Airbnb business make sure you guys hit
that like button I would really appreciate it and here's the thing guys whenever you hit the like
button it tells the YouTube algorithm that this video is great that you liked it and what they
do is they will show it to more people looking to get started with their short-term rental business
so thank you so much in advance for hitting that like button the next objection that the owner
might have is that they don't understand the regulation so they might be you know concerned
about hey can you even run a short-term rental in this city do you need a permit do I as the owner
need to apply for the permit or is it going to be you and so what you want to do here is maybe
forward them with their regulation and ordinance is which you can find online or simply calling the
local building department in that City and let's say for example that the city does issue permits
all they might need is a notarized document from the owner giving you permission which is often the
case in cities where you need a permit and then boom straightforward it's just about educating
them in the process the fifth objection that may come up is that the landlord doesn't want
to be responsible for replacing any furniture or appliances that are left in the property when you
take over in my experience most large appliances will already be in the unit although not always
what is very rare is that winning property is already furnished and you can take over
the property and keep the furniture so let's say there's a couch that's been at this property for
three years the owner moved out they got all new stuff and they just left the property furnished
which is great because it keeps more money in your pocket well if the furniture has any type
of issues wear and tear or it breaks they're not going to be responsible for them as they
shouldn't so typically I will put in writing that if there's any Replacements or repairs
that needs to happen to any of the furniture or appliances I as the person subleasing the
property will be responsible to replace or repair as needed subleasing is the most effective way to
replace a nine to five and to create Financial Freedom so if you are ready now to start your
business and you have the capital to be able to do so I want to invite you to set up a free
15-minute consultation with my team to see if I could be your coach mentor and personally Hold
Your Hand every step of the way to launch your first Airbnb in the next 30 to 45 days all you
need to do is click on the link Down Below in the description and schedule your free consultation I
also invite you guys to follow me on Instagram at the Jorge Contreras that's t-h-e Jorge Contreras
where I post every single day and also I do have a podcast that you can find on iTunes the Jorge
Contreras show where we post episodes every single week and before you guys go anywhere
make sure you guys check out one of the other videos here on my channel see you on the next one

metadata.shortDescription:
Download at http://rentalleaseagreement.org/sublease/

Use this document to create a sublease agreement between a person that is currently under a lease agreement and a person that is seeking to rent the same space. This type of rental arrangement is common among urban developments with more than one roommate and college campuses when a student returns home for the summer and/or holidays.

The Landlord should always be notified of the new rental arrangement unless it is specifically allowed in the original lease. It must be known by all parties that the original Tenant is responsible for all payments until the end of his or her agreement with the Landlord.

Students studying for their real estate exam must know the two key real estate terms discussed in this video: ASSIGNMENT OF LEASE and SUBLEASING. 

Key real estate terms:

(1) Assignment of Lease - Lessee (tenant) transfers all rights and priviledges held under the lease agreement to the new lessee.
(2) Subleasing (sublet) - Lessee retains original lease but rents all or a portion of the premises to a sublessee (subtenant)
(3) Lessor (landlord) - The owner of a rental property that has been leased to another. Holder has leasehold interests in the property.
(4) Lessee (tenant) - The tenant who is party to a lease agreement with the lessor 
(5) Assignor - The person who assigns their interest in a contract to another called the assignee
(6) Assignee - The person who is receiving the interest in a contract of another called the assignor

metadata.title: Renting Out Your House Your Homeowners Insurance Probably Doesn't Cover It
metadata.author: Real Property Management Palisade
metadata.shortDescription:
Thinking about renting out your home? Before your tenants move in, there's one important thing I want you to check. 🏡

Many homeowners assume their existing homeowners insurance will continue to protect their property once they start renting it out. Unfortunately, that isn't always the case.

In this video, I explain why a standard homeowners insurance policy may not provide the coverage you need when your home becomes a rental property.

I'll also discuss why it's important to understand the difference between homeowners and landlord insurance, what risks you should be aware of, and why reviewing your coverage before handing over the keys can help prevent costly surprises.

Whether you're renting out your former home or preparing to become a landlord for the first time, making sure you have the right insurance is an important part of protecting your investment.

The big thing to remember is that an insurance policy for the home you live in may not be designed for the same risks once someone else is living there as a tenant. Coverage can depend on the insurer, the policy wording, and how the property is being used.

Landlord insurance is worth discussing with your provider because rental properties can come with different risks, including property damage, liability, and potential loss of rental income. What is covered, and under what circumstances, varies by policy. You don't want to assume a claim will be paid only to discover an exclusion later.

Before you rent out the property, tell your insurance provider about your plans, ask what your current policy covers, and find out whether you need different protection. It's also sensible to review coverage when the property is vacant between tenants, since vacancy can affect the terms of a policy.

Planning to rent out your property in New Jersey? Get in touch with me at Real Property Management Palisade to learn how we can help you manage your rental.

🌐 https://rpmpalisade.com

#NewJerseyLandlords #LandlordInsurance #RentalProperty #PropertyManagement #LandlordTips

metadata.author: Steadily

Chapters:
0:00 What is the difference between homeowner insurance and landlord insurance?
0:12 What is homeowner insurance?
0:50 What is landlord insurance?
1:33 Which type of insurance costs more?
2:04 How can landlords reduce the cost of their insurance?
2:47 Find out more

First, it's important to purchase the right kind of insurance policy for the usage type. In fact, whether a claim is covered may depend on having the right type of policy in place. As an example, if you decided to open a car rental business and buy a fleet of cars, you wouldn’t insure the rental cars on your personal auto policy. The risks are different — and the insurer won’t cover claims because the policy doesn’t match the real risks. Insuring your investment real estate follows the same logic. Even for a single-family home you lived in previously, if you decide to rent the home out, the risks change. You’ll need a landlord insurance policy for long-term rentals. Frequent short-term rentals need special coverage as well.

Landlord insurance covers similar risks to those that homeowners insurance covers, but there are still some key differences. Many landlord insurance policies are all-risk policies that cover all types of property damage — except for those excluded by the policy. Exclusions are often limited to preventable losses, such as neglect or intentional property damage, and risks tied to location, such as earthquake or flood coverage.

Expect coverage for common risks such as fire, theft, vandalism, and many types of water damage, although flood damage typically requires a separate policy. However, your landlord insurance policy also offers expanded liability protection, often with higher limits than you’ll find on a standard home insurance policy. Investment property owners have more to protect and potentially face greater exposure because renters may not be as careful with the property.

A helpful way to view the difference between homeowners insurance cost and landlord insurance cost is to think of your homeowners insurance policy earning a discount because the property is your primary residence. Your insurer has a greater assurance that you’ll be on guard against risks and take precautions to prevent claims if the property is owner-occupied.

While these property insurance types are similar, your homeowners insurance company may not offer landlord insurance. Again, this is likely because the risks are different based on who lives in the home.

exposed. Hey everyone, welcome back to the channel. Today we're diving into a topic
every landlord, whether you have one rental or a whole portfolio, absolutely needs to understand,
the difference between homeowners insurance and landlord insurance. This is the one of the most
common mistakes new landlords make and it can cost thousands of dollars if something goes wrong. So,
let's break it down clearly, simply, and make sure you're protected. Hi, I'm Sylvia White,
new client adviser at Blue Fox Properties. Whether you manage one rental or an entire portfolio, this
video will help you stay compliant, protect your investment, and set everyone up for success. So,
here's the thing. Once you turn your home into a rental, your insurance needs to change. A
homeowner's policy is not designed for tenant occupied properties. Claims get denied every
single day because the wrong policy was in place. And the worst part, most landlords don't find out
until after a major loss. My goal today is to make sure that never happens to you. Let's start with
homeowners insurance. Homeowners insurance is built for one specific situation. You live in
the home. It covers the structure, your personal belongings, your liability if a guest gets hurt,
and damage from things like fire, storms, or theft. But here's the problem. Once a tenant
moves in, almost everything about that policy becomes misaligned with how the home is actually
being used. Your belongings aren't in the home. Your liability changes and tenant cause damage
often isn't covered. So, if you're renting out the property, homeowners insurance is no longer
the correct policy. Now, before we move on, if you don't want to deal with managing your rental
property, contact us about managing your rental home. we may be the perfect fit to take this
off your plate so you can enjoy the benefits of owning rental property without the stress. Now,
let's talk about landlord insurance, sometimes called dwelling policy or a DP3 policy. Landlord
insurance is designed specifically for rental properties. It assumes tenants live there, not
you. And it covers the risks that come with that. First, it covers the structure, fire, storms,
vandalism, burst pipes, all the major perils you'd expect. This part is similar to homeowners
insurance, but the poly is policy is written for a rental, which is key. Second, it includes landlord
liability protection. If a tenant or guest gets hurt because of a condition on the property,
maybe a loose handrail or step that breaks, landlord liability helps protect you from
lawsuits, medical bills, and legal fees. Third, it includes loss of rent coverage. This is a big
one. If the home becomes uninhabitable due to a covered loss, like a fire or major water damage,
loss of rent coverage reimbures you for the rental income you're missing while the repairs are being
made. Fourth, it covers limited personal property. This means items you provide for the tenants use
like appliances, window coverings, light fixtures. It does not cover your personal belongings because
those aren't part of the rental. Now, let's talk about the must-have protections you want to make
sure are included in your landlord policy. Not all policies are created equal, so this part
is really important. Number one, replacement cost coverage. This ensures repairs are paid
out at today's prices, not depreciated value. You always want replacement cost. Number two,
extended or guaranteed dwelling coverage. Construction costs can spike. This coverage
gives you a buffer if repairs end up costing more than your policy limit. Number three,
ordinance and law coverage. If your home needs code upgrades during repairs, which
is extremely common in older homes, this coverage pays for those required improvements. Number four,
water damage and sewer backup coverage. This is often optional, but is absolutely critical. Sewer
backups or water intrusion can cause thousands of dollars in damage, and without this endorsement,
you are paying out of pocket. Number five, loss of rent coverage. Make sure
it's included and make sure the amount matches your market's current rental rate. Number six,
strong liability limits. We recommend at least 500,000 in liability coverage. Many landlords go
even higher or add an umbrella policy for extra protection. Number seven, coverage for tenant
cause damage. Some policies offer endorsements for accidental tenant damage. If it's available,
it's worth considering. Now, let's talk about something just as important as having the right
policy. Making sure your property meets basic safety requirements. Insurance companies can and
do deny claims when safety items are missing or not up to code. Number one, working smoke alarms
in all required locations, hallways, bedrooms, and common areas. Test them regularly. Missing
smoke alarms is one of the fastest ways to get a claim denied. Number two, no dual cylinder
deadbolts. These require key from the inside and are considered a fire hazard. Insurance companies
can deny liability claims if tenants can't exit quickly during an emergency. Number three, screens
on all operable windows. Screens help prevent falls, keep pests out, and maintain habitability.
Missing screens can be cited as a contributing factor in liability claims. Number four, properly
functioning locks and egress points. Doors and windows must open easily and safely. Anything that
restricts emergency exit can cause issues during a claim. Number five, compliance with local building
and fire codes. Insurance companies expect rentals to meet minimum safety standards. If something is
out of compliance, it can complicate or reduce a payout. Bottom line, safety isn't just about
protecting tenants. It's about protecting your insurance coverage. So, here's the bottom line.
If you have the wrong policy, your claim can be denied, and that can be financially devastating.
Landlord insurance protects your investment, your liability, and your rental income. It's
designed for the real risks that come with tenants living in the home. Having the right
coverage isn't just smart, it's essential. If you found this helpful, hit like, subscribe,
and drop your questions in the comments. Whether you're a brand new landlord or you've been doing

your property and your financial future. Thank you for watching and I'll see you in the next

metadata.author: Bryan Gutowsky | Michigan Insurance

Rental Property Insurance vs Homeowners Insurance – What You Need To Know

If you own a rental property or are thinking about buying one, understanding the difference between rental property insurance and a standard homeowners policy is essential. While they share many similarities, there are key differences in how coverage applies — especially when the property is tenant-occupied instead of owner-occupied.

In this video, we’ll break down:
🔹 What’s the same between homeowners and rental property insurance
🔹 Why rental property insurance (or a Dwelling Fire policy) is needed for tenant-occupied homes
🔹 To make sure your property is insured to replacement cost value — not market value
🔹 The difference in personal property coverage limits between the two policies
🔹 Why a rental property policy can cost more and the main reasons why
🔹 The importance of listing the correct named insured if the property is owned by an LLC or trust
🔹 Why you should require tenants to carry renters insurance
🔹 How an umbrella policy can add an extra layer of protection for landlords

Whether you’re managing one rental or a portfolio of properties, understanding these differences ensures your coverage actually matches how the property is being used — and protects you from costly surprises down the road.
