So, this is why having those higher limits for your liability coverage or potentially adding an umbrella policy can be very important. And now, as far as cost goes, unfortunately, a rental property insurance policy will typically be a little bit more expensive than a traditional homeowner's policy. The insurance companies see this as a higher risk exposure when you aren't the actual one living there on a day-to-day basis. So, as you can see, rental property insurance and a homeowner's policy will be built on very similar foundations, and a lot of the coverages will be the same, but they are definitely not interchangeable. And it is important to make sure that you do have the right coverage in place if your home is being rented out. So, thank you for watching. And if you are looking for help with your rental property insurance or just insurance in general, I would love the opportunity to see if our team can help. There are a lot of ways to get a hold of me and they should all be in the description below. Please feel free to text, call, email, fill out a contact form, whatever is easiest. And if you have any other questions about insurance, please feel free to reach out directly or leave them in the comments below. I would love to help answer those as well. So, thank you again.

metadata.shortDescription:
THINKING OF STARTING AN AIRBNB IN THE UNITED STATES?

Here's something every vacation rental owner needs to understand: There is no single nationwide set of short-term rental rules.

What's allowed in one city may be restricted or require additional permits in another.

📍 Here's what every US Airbnb host should know:

🏠 Licensing & Registration: Your city or county may require permits before you can legally operate.

📋 Zoning Restrictions: Some neighborhoods limit or prohibit short-term rentals.

💰 Taxes: Rental income may be subject to federal income tax and applicable state or local lodging taxes.

🔥 Safety Standards: Fire safety, occupancy limits, and other property requirements can apply.

⚖️ Consumer Protection: Hosts must follow applicable advertising, pricing transparency, and anti-discrimination laws.

Whether you own a vacation home, manage multiple Airbnb properties, or rent out a spare room, understanding your local regulations is essential.

Don't assume your property is compliant just because you've hosted guests before.

🔗 Get a location-specific property compliance report at lodgecompliance.com

📌 Save this post and share it with another Airbnb host!

#AirbnbUSA #ShortTermRentalLaws #AirbnbRegulations #VacationRentalManagement #AirbnbBusiness #RealEstateInvesting #STRCompliance #LodgeCompliance

segments.text: For millions of travelers, the United
States is where vacation dreams come
true, offering endless possibilities for
unforgettable travel experiences, many
of them powered by short-term rentals
that serve as a home away from home,
providing flexibility and a sense of
belonging beyond traditional hotels.
In the US, short-term rentals are often
called vacation rentals or transient
accommodations, and generally refer to
properties rented for less than 30 days
at a time.
These include everything from cozy
cabins and spare rooms to luxury condos
and entire homes, offering temporary
housing for travelers, business guests,
and families alike.
But here's the catch.
There is no single rulebook.
The maximum length of stay that
qualifies as a short-term rental varies
by location.
In many states, it ranges from 30 to 90
days, and in some places even up to 120
days, depending on local regulations. In
states like South Dakota, Vermont, and
Wisconsin, certain short-term rental
rules may not apply at all unless the
property is rented for more than 7 to 14
days per year.
Short-term rental laws in the US are as
diverse as the landscapes themselves.
Every state, and often every city,
country, or even neighborhood sets its
own rules.
These may include registration or
licensing requirements, zoning
restrictions, safety standards, and
occupancy limits.
And then there are taxes.
Income generated from short-term rentals
in the United States is taxable and
generally must be reported if the
property is rented for more than 14 days
in a calendar year.
Hosts may be able to deduct certain
rental-related expenses, such as
maintenance, utilities, insurance, and
property management fees.
However, if a host provides additional
services like frequent cleaning during a
stay, guided tours, meals, or
concierge-style services, the IRS may
classify that activity as
self-employment, which can trigger
self-employment taxes.
There is also no national lodging tax.
Instead, states and local governments
impose occupancy taxes, sales taxes,
lodging taxes, or room taxes, depending
on where the property is located.
Tax rates vary widely.
For example, Maine has a statewide
lodging tax of 9%, while Maryland
applies both state and local lodging
taxes.
In major cities like Chicago, combined
short-term rental taxes can exceed 21%.
Beyond taxes, compliance also includes
federal legal obligations.
Short-term rental hosts must follow
federal anti-discrimination laws,
including the Fair Housing Act and the
Americans with Disabilities Act, ADA.
These laws prohibit discrimination based
on protected characteristics and help
ensure that short-term rentals remain
fair, accessible, and inclusive.
Hosts are also subject to federal
consumer protection laws, including the
Federal Trade Commission, FTC, Act and
the No Hidden Fees Act, which require
transparent pricing and prohibit
deceptive advertising.
Guests must be shown the total leasing
price upfront, including all mandatory
fees, such as cleaning fees, service
fees, and taxes.
The good news?
You are not alone.
There are strong communities of
short-term rental owners, both online
and in person, where hosts share
insights, experiences, and compliance
tips.
If you're hosting or thinking about
hosting in the United States, you need
to confirm whether short-term rentals
are legal and which regulations apply to
your specific property, as several years
of hosting does not guarantee
compliance.
Get your property report today.

In this episode, Jon Bell and Julian Sage dive into crafting bullet-proof rental agreements—showing you which clauses to include so you’re protected if a pandemic or recession strikes.

You’ll learn how to:

Define a robust force-majeure clause: Specify events (pandemics, government shutdowns) that allow rent relief or lease suspension without penalty.

Include rent-deferral mechanisms: Build in options for temporary payment pauses or amortized catch-up schedules triggered by financial hardship.

Add early-termination rights: Outline clear break-clause procedures—notice periods, penalty caps, and exit conditions—to minimize lock-in risk.

Require business-interruption insurance: Mandate policy coverage for revenue losses, ensuring claims can cover rent and operating costs during downturns.

Embed health & safety protocols: Formalize enhanced cleaning standards and tenant cooperation clauses so both parties share responsibility for compliance.

Plan for rent reviews & adjustments: Schedule regular market-rate assessments and include formula-based adjustments to align rent with economic realities.

By the end of this episode, you’ll have a fail-safe rental agreement framework—so you can weather economic shocks, keep your cash flow healthy, and host with confidence.

metadata.title: Travel Nurses and Contract Workers: The Co-Living Guest Who Pays More (Guest Type 2 of 7)
metadata.author: The CoLiving Insider
metadata.shortDescription:
Travel nurses and traveling contract workers arrive with a suitcase, a paycheck, and often a housing stipend. They need a home in days, not weeks, and they will pay more for a room that is ready the moment they walk in. But they also leave every few months, and demand can rise and fall with a single hospital or job site. In this second episode of our guest type series, you will learn who these guests are, what your house needs, where to find them, and how to tell if your house is a good fit.

In this video:
0:00 Intro: the guest who pays with tax-free money
0:34 Who travel nurses are
1:09 How housing stipends work, and why this guest can pay more
1:28 Who traveling contract workers are 
1:51 The data center boom and the crews that follow it
2:51 The Guest Card: stay length, turnover, management load, and setup cost
3:27 What the house needs to be ready on day one
5:08 The mistake that leaves rooms empty every thirteen weeks
5:59 The best location, and the one question to ask a hospital before you buy
6:47 Pros and cons for the operator 
7:28 The best marketing channels for nurses and for crews
8:46 Which guests fit beside them when a room sits empty
9:40 Your Plan B
10:22 The five-question Home Fit Check

Start with the series overview: 
Who Actually Rents Rooms? https://youtu.be/W76TqF_XRVs Guest Type 1: Workforce and Essential Workers https://youtu.be/144iA0ZIzCo 
Full guest type framework: https://ralphpombo.com/guest-types 
Next up, Guest Type 3: young professionals. Subscribe so you do not miss it.

Is there a hospital or a big job site near your house? Tell us in the comments.

Travel nurse staffing agencies to contact. Call their housing or recruiter teams, tell them you have furnished rooms near the hospital, and build the relationship: 
Aya Healthcare, the largest travel nurse staffing firm in the U.S. (Staffing Industry Analysts, 2026): https://www.ayahealthcare.com 
Medical Solutions, one of the top two travel nursing firms (Staffing Industry Analysts, 2025): https://www.medicalsolutions.com 
AMN Healthcare, one of the five largest U.S. healthcare staffing firms (Staffing Industry Analysts, 2026): https://www.amnhealthcare.com 
Trusted Health, ranked 13th among U.S. travel nurse staffing firms (Staffing Industry Analysts, 2026): https://www.trustedhealth.com 
Also ask your local hospital which agencies it uses. Regional agencies can be just as valuable.

Sources: Staffing Industry Analysts, travel nurse staffing forecast, October 2026: https://www.staffingindustry.com/news/global-daily-news/travel-nurse-staffing-turning-corner-with-2-growth 
Health Resources and Services Administration, 2022 National Sample Survey of Registered Nurses: https://content.govdelivery.com/attachments/IACIO/2024/04/18/file_attachments/2851137/Nurse-Survey-Fact-Sheet-2024.pdf 
Furnished Finder, why rent to travel nurses: https://www.furnishedfinder.com/blog/why-rent-to-travel-nurses 
Advantis Medical, travel nurse tax home and stipend rules: https://advantismed.com/blog/travel-nurse-tax-home 
Staffing Industry Analysts, largest U.S. healthcare staffing firms, 2026 update: https://www.staffingindustry.com/news/global-daily-news/largest-us-healthcare-staffing-firms-generate-33b-in-revenue 
Insurance Journal (Bloomberg), data center construction workers and temporary housing: https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/southcentral/2026/03/06/860884.htm

This video is for education only and is not legal, tax, or financial advice. Follow fair housing law and your local rules.

The Co-Living Insider covers the co-living and shared housing model for real estate investors and operators.

#CoLiving #TravelNurseHousing #realestateinvestingwithnomoney

metadata.title: The Corporate Housing Revolution Why Flexibility, and Human Centered Design Are Winning
metadata.author: PBD Living | Furnished Housing
metadata.shortDescription:
Corporate housing is undergoing a massive shift—and traditional hotels and short-term rentals are struggling to keep up.

In this video, we break down The Corporate Housing Revolution and why flexibility, human-centered design, and purpose-built living experiences are winning in today’s relocation, workforce, and insurance housing markets.

At PBD Living, we work directly with:
✔ Traveling professionals
✔ Corporate relocation teams
✔ Insurance adjusters & displaced families
✔ Medical professionals & interns
✔ Companies needing flexible, fully-furnished housing

What we’re seeing is clear: people no longer want “a place to stay”—they want a place to live.

In this video, you’ll learn:

Why corporate housing demand is exploding in 2025 into 2026
The difference between short-term rentals vs. mid-term corporate housing
How human-centered design increases retention and reduces turnover
Why flexibility beats long leases and rigid hotel contracts
What owners and investors need to know to stay competitive

Whether you’re a property owner, investor, HR professional, relocation manager, or traveling professional, this video explains why the future of housing is flexible, furnished, and hospitality-driven.

#CorporateHousing #FlexibleLiving #MidTermRentals #RelocationHousing #FurnishedHousing #PBDLiving

🔗 Relevant Links

🌐 Learn more about PBD Living:
👉 https://www.pbdliving.com

🏠 Looking for Corporate or Mid-Term Housing in Dallas–Fort Worth?
👉 https://www.pbdliving.com

🤝 Property Owners – Partner With Us:
👉 https://www.pbdliving.com/owners

📩 Direct Inquiries:
Email: info@pbdliving.com

📍 Serving Dallas–Fort Worth | Nationwide Placements Available

segments.text: The way we live and work has changed
forever. And in the world of corporate
housing, 2025 is proving to be the year
that short and midterm housing providers
must evolve or risk becoming obsolete.
Gone are the days of cookie cutter hotel
suites and rigid leases. Today's
business traveler, relocating family, or
insurance displaced guest expects more
than just a roof over their head. They
demand personalized comfort, seamless
digital experiences, and an ethos of
sustainability.
At PBD Living, we've seen these trends
not only take root, but define what
success looks like in this evolving
landscape. So, what's changing and what
does it mean for the future of corporate
and temporary housing?
One, the rise of flexible living for
real life moments. Work trips are
longer. Insurance claims are more
complex. Life transitions are more
frequent. That's why flexible housing
models, those offering 30 to 90day stays
with no long-term commitments, are
booming. Midterm rentals, MTRS, have
become the ideal solution for traveling
nurses and medical professionals staying
near hospitals during contract
assignments, displaced families who need
a temporary home after storm, fire, or
flood damage, interns and remote
employees working in unfamiliar cities,
relocation clients transitioning between
cities or awaiting permanent homes. At
PBD Living, nearly 80% of our bookings
are now for 30 plus nights. And with
platforms like Furnished Finder, Airbnb,
and our own direct booking site, we've
made it easier than ever for guests to
find what they need without the
headaches of a 12-month lease.
Two, hospitality over real estate.
One of the most exciting shifts in our
industry is the move away from property
management toward hospitality first
operations.
Guests don't just want a clean home.
They want thoughtful welcome baskets,
smart home tech, reliable service, and
real-time support when something goes
wrong. In 2025, the companies thriving
in corporate housing are the ones that
operate more like boutique hotels than
landlords. 247 virtual concierge,
digital check-in plus digital house
manuals, local recommendations through
VAR and other curated partnerships,
in-home amenities like Pelatons,
ergonomic desks or espresso machines,
fast empathetic resolutions to
maintenance or service issues. As one
guest told us after relocating from New
Jersey during her husband's surgery,
"You made a difficult life moment feel
like a luxury station. I'll never forget
that." Three, sustainability is a
non-negotiable. Sustainable travel isn't
a trend, it's an expectation. At PBD
Living, we've made the commitment to
become the first carbonneutral corporate
housing company in Texas, offsetting
100% of the energy consumed in our
homes. But we're not alone. Across the
industry, operators are beginning to
invest in energy efficient appliances
and LED lighting offer recycling
stations and composting kits. Track and
offset carbon usage using platforms like
green places. Educate guests on ways to
reduce waste during their stay. Choose
local eco-conscious vendors for
housekeeping and supplies. This isn't
just good PR, it's good business.
Corporate clients now prioritize vendors
with strong ESG commitments, and
relocation partners are selecting
housing partners who align with their
values. Four, direct booking equals
direct control. If you're still relying
solely on Airbnb or VBO in 2025, you're
playing defense. Yes, OTAAS, online
travel agencies, bring visibility, but
they also take a cut of the revenue,
control cancellation policies, and
insert friction between you and your
guest. That's why direct booking
platforms are critical for brand control
and profitability. Our team has
implemented a direct booking strategy
using HYI to accept secure reservations
and offer discounted rates. Custom
landing pages with lead magnets like
stay 30 nights get three free. Facebook
and LinkedIn ads targeted to insurance
adjusters, traveling professionals, and
HR reps. An affiliate referral program
that rewards realtors and relocation
agents. automated email marketing
campaigns for past guests and leads.
Result: higher margins, longer stays,
and stronger relationships with our
clients. Five, community is the ultimate
differentiator.
Technology can't replace human warmth.
Whether we're housing a family who lost
everything in a fire or welcoming a solo
traveler to a new city, our job is to
create connection. That means going
beyond Wi-Fi passwords and thermostat
instructions. It means offering
neighborhood guides with our favorite
restaurants, sunrise spots, and coffee
shops. Hosting networking events for
guests staying in the same area, leaving
handwritten notes and care packages
after long flights or surgeries,
listening deeply, and responding quickly
even when it's not our fault. As an
African-American woman-ledd company, we
also take pride in representing
diversity in hospitality,
making sure that every guest, regardless
of race, orientation, or background,
feels seen, safe, and welcomed.
Now, what comes next? As corporate
housing professionals, we are no longer
just operators. We are experienced
architects, tech innovators, and
community builders. If you're in this
space, the message is clear. Stay
flexible. Lead with hospitality. Build
your own brand. Go green on purpose. Be
radically human. And if you're a guest
or relocation partner looking for
housing that actually feels like home,
we invite you to explore how companies
like PBD Living are reshaping what's
possible. Because people don't just want
a place to stay, they want a place where
they can thrive.

metadata.shortDescription:
What if you could keep the income of short term rentals but lose most of the daily work? There is a powerful middle ground between Airbnb and long term rentals that most investors completely overlook. In this episode of Landlord Diaries, we sit down with Tim Hubbard, CEO of Corzly and host of the Short Term Rental Riches podcast, to unpack why experienced short term rental investors are adding midterm rentals.

Tim has hosted more than 50,000 guests across 10 countries and manages more than 200 properties worldwide. His portfolio includes both short term rentals and monthly furnished rentals, giving him a unique perspective on how investors can blend both strategies for stronger returns, fewer vacancies, and simpler operations.

You will learn why many landlords are discovering that midterm rentals are the sweet spot between short term and long term leasing. With monthly tenants staying an average of around 100 days on Furnished Finder, landlords can enjoy steady income with far fewer turnovers.

We also explore how investors manage furnished rentals from hundreds or even thousands of miles away, how to pivot properties seasonally between STR and MTR, and why platforms like Furnished Finder are becoming essential for landlords looking to capture growing demand from traveling professionals, relocating families, travel nurses and more.

Furnished Finder currently connects more than 240,000 landlords with over 6 million travelers each year looking for monthly housing, making it the largest platforms dedicated to midterm rentals.

If you are a real estate investor, Airbnb host, or landlord looking to stabilize income while reducing operational headaches, this conversation will show you how monthly furnished rentals can fit into your portfolio.


In this episode you will learn:
- Why midterm rentals are often the most overlooked real estate strategy
- How to manage furnished rentals remotely from anywhere in the world
- When to use short term rentals vs monthly rentals based on seasonality
- Policies every landlord should include in a midterm lease
- How Furnished Finder helps landlords fill longer stays with qualified tenants


List your property on Furnished Finder now:
https://www.furnishedfinder.com/list-your-property 
Use code LLD10 for $10 off new listings.

Monthly rental resources:
https://www.furnishedfinder.com/Resources/PMResources

What piece of advice would you give them? >> Well, I'd say it's easier to do now than it's ever been in history, you know, and it and it's getting easier and it's getting more common, you know, so the more if they just reach out on a local group, I think that they would find that there's lots of people that have those same fears that are now renting remotely and they love it, you know, and and it's working out really well. It does, of course, require that you have a really good contact there on the ground. It could just be a housekeeper, you know, but it's nice to have a handyman there as well, a go-to person, you know, if something does come up. And after you've made that connection, then and that's really reassuring. I mean, and and really after you go through a couple rentals, that's it, you know, you see that it's not this big scary thing where people are going to show up and destroy your property and you know, it's uh Um I think another nice thing with with the space is that you get paid up front, too, you know, so um that's always that's always reassuring, but yeah, I would say just just take a peek around, you know, there's lots and lots of people doing it remotely now and yeah, it doesn't matter if you're 100 miles away or 1,000 miles away. There's more tools than there's ever been and and it's easier than it's ever been. But it's not easy. What's your crystal ball say when it comes to midterms? >> I would say that there's going to be a lot more short-term rentals. They're going to start offering mid-term stays. For multiple reasons. One, which we've talked about is that there's just less operations. But another one would be that supply on the short-term rental side of things has really increased in a lot of places to the point where there's way more competition for short-term rentals than there might be for mid-term rentals. >> All right. Well, we like to wrap up our episodes with a few fun rapid-fire questions that you can just whatever comes to mind, feel free and just share them with us. Doesn't have to be deep thoughts, but you know, part of the remote management life is that a lot of landlords value is that freedom, right? So, if you have a freedom, what are you going to do with that time? Like, what is Tim's go-to of how he detoxes, relaxes, and just enjoys life? >> Good question. So, for a really long time, that was just traveling. I just traveled and traveled all over the place, and that's how I got into the space, you know, staying in a lot of furnished rentals. People are living differently now. People are living in short-term rentals, or living in mid-term rentals, and they used to not do that as much. They weren't available They weren't able to with, you know, having to be in an office, but I would say with my free time, I'm traveling less, but I'm playing more tennis. I really like tennis. >> I really respect the fact that you said tennis and not pickleball. I have nothing against pickleball. In fact, I have yet to play it. I can never find time in my calendar between work and kids and the growing list of activities that my kids are involved in. But I It's just I feel like you and Kelly actually are both the tennis >> It's amazing. Yes. Don't be dissing pickleball, Katie. >> right? I'm here for like like the tried and true. I don't need pickleball. Just give me tennis. I need it. >> I've been playing tennis since I was born, and I need pickleball, too. >> Yeah, that's awesome. >> I love it. All right, next rapid-fire question. What is the biggest mistake new hosts make when they are managing remotely? >> Um not having backups. So, maybe they do have a handyman or someone that can go there, but maybe there's an issue that needs to be handled right away, and they haven't found a backup. And that person's not available right then, or maybe they just didn't ask that question in the beginning. Like, how much notice do you actually need? So, I would say um not having backups. Backup contacts. >> And backups for your backups. >> Right. >> And backup batteries. Dang it. Have some backup batteries. >> batteries. >> got a smart lock, backup batteries, and smoke alarms. Yeah. >> Quick quick little tip I I I learned along the way uh um is having what Jasper Rivers called, I think, an ammo box. Uh he's he's from the short-term rental side, but nothing to do with ammunition, but having a box or something hidden somewhere in the property. >> Like a tackle box that has extra batteries, has, you know, screwdrivers, has light bulbs, has these like basic things that you might have to send a a handyman out for when someone could just as easily uh swap that out, you know what I'm saying? Yeah. >> A lot of times people are people are happy to help out swapping batteries or light bulbs or whatever it may be if it means they can just get it done and not have to deal with a scheduling appointment. >> or a stool like a ladder or a three-step stool because how many times do you have the battery, but you can't reach the ceiling where the smoke alarm is. So, giving them the means to be able to reach whatever it is they need to reach. >> Yeah. Yeah, I love it. All right, last rapid-fire question. What is one policy you wish every landlord would add to their lease? This is going to be interesting cuz you're coming from the short-term rental perspective. That's why I think these these answers are are so interesting because I feel like sometimes y'all are more prepared than us by default sometimes. >> We've got a long list of of things that we've added over the years. One thing I would put in that that notice piece, you know, making sure making sure that they know up front that like, "Hey, I I can't reserve this property for you if if your plans are uncertain, but I would love to, and so we'll hold it for this amount of time, but I have to know by this time, otherwise I'll open the calendar." Um I would say that one because I think people are moving to mid-term rentals at the end of the day to to make more money than they're earning with their long-term rentals. And if their calendar's not staying full, then you know, that's that's that's where they make the money, so I would I would say that one. >> Kelly, what's yours? What's one policy you wish every landlord had in their lease? >> I I add the move-in and move-out time, right? I put a 4:00 p.m. move-in and a 10:00 a.m. check-out because by default uh a lot of leases don't have a time. They just it's a day, right? And so we work off nightly uh the nightly calendar. So, that's what I would add to that's what I add to every lease that um is helpful, and then it makes you look like the hero. You're like, "Oh, hey, guess what? You know, we actually don't have an anyone checking in later today. You can leave whenever you like. So, then it's like a nice little icing on the cake whenever they're checking out if you have a little freedom there and you and you have a day or two in between. >> I've got two and both of them are pretty new for me as a landlord. So, if there is a pest that's five doors down, we're doing pest control whether you like it or not. >> [laughter] >> Not optional. So, with a short-term, you know, you could do those in between tenants, but I don't always want to wait 60 days for the next person. So, All right, Tim. This was fantastic. I always love getting to talk to someone from the short-term world because, you know, it's just it's like a little pivot of the perspective. It's not an entirely different perspective. It's just like a little bit of a of a of an adjustment. Um and I agree with you. I think that Kelly and I both see short-term rental hosts just flooding into the mid-term rental world, especially those in seasonal markets or really looking to book up that calendar and and take it advantage of the opportunity there. So, remind everybody how to connect with you if you would like and how to learn more from you because um you have a slew of information that is available for free and at the fingertips of users. >> Yep. Yep. Um so, I have a podcast called Short Term Rental Riches. I think it's been over 6 years now. So, every Tuesday, uh we've got a quick actionable episode to help with short-term rentals, but we've talked about mid-term rentals a lot and we talked about just investing in general a lot. Uh our management company is called Coursely, c o r z l y. So, strriches.com is the podcast website or and coursely.com is our our management site. >> Awesome. Well, thank you so much for being with us today. metadata.title: MTR vs. Airbnb: How Savvy Investors Are Pivoting for 2026
metadata.author: NickProRealty
metadata.shortDescription:
The "perfect Airbnb machine" is breaking. In 2026, savvy residential investors are quietly shifting their strategy from short-term volatility to mid-term stability.

In this episode of *The Property Code,* we break down why Mid-Term Rentals (MTRs) are outperforming Airbnbs for sophisticated investors right now. From tightening city regulations and rising insurance costs to the "fragility" of the short-term model, the game has changed.

*What you’ll learn in this video:*

*  The Fragility Factor: Why a high-sensitivity Airbnb machine is risky in 2026.
*  The Tenant Profile: Why travel nurses, corporate relocations, and families in transition are the "quality" tenants you want.
*  Operational Pivot: How to design for durability over aesthetics and why your screening process needs to look more like traditional leasing.
*  Risk-Adjusted Returns: Why stable years beat highest-possible months every time.

Whether you are in Tampa, Miami, or any major metro area, building a resilient income stream means trading volatility for control.

---

*Timestamps*

0:00 — Welcome to The Property Code 
0:24 — 2026 Search Trends: What renters are actually looking for 
1:12 — The Ryan Case Study: When the Airbnb rules changed 
2:25 — The Pivot: Chasing months instead of chasing weekends 
2:48 — Who is the MTR tenant? (Nurses, Corp Relo, and more) 
4:07 — Why Mid-Term Rentals reduce portfolio fragility 
5:20 — Navigating regulations and neighborhood friction 
5:41 — The hidden benefit: Reducing wear and tear 
6:02 — Product Design: Furnishing for durability, not just "the gram" 
6:48 — MTR Screening: Trading quantity for quality 
8:40 — Risk-Adjusted Returns vs. Peak Revenue 
9:53 — Building a resilient, flexible asset in 2026 
---
🔗 *Connect with Nick Polyushkin:*
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/nick.pro.33
Instagram: https://instagram.com/nickprorealty?utm_medium=copy_link

segments.text: Welcome to the property code. I am Nick
and today we are talking about something
that is quietly reshaping residential
investing as we move through 2026. Why
midterm rentals are outperforming
Airbnbs for savvy real estate investors
right now. Before we get into the story,
I need to anchor the demand you are
seeing in search. I do not have your
screenshot in this chat, so I cannot
quote it directly. But the most common
highintense searches tied to this topic
in 2026 cluster into four buckets.
First, people search mid-term rentals
and corporate housing because they want
longer stays without going fully
long-term. Second, they search Airbnb
regulations and short-term rental bans
because rules keep tightening in many
cities and enforcement is getting real.
Third, they search travel, nurse
housing, and furnished rentals because
demand is tied to healthcare, corporate
relocation, and life transitions.
Fourth, they search how to furnish a
rental and how to price a midterm rental
because the operational playbook is
different. Consider that demand mapping
a working hypothesis. You can align your
script to even without the exact
screenshot. Now, the story. Meet Ryan.
He is 39, lives in Tampa, and thought he
had built the perfect Airbnb machine.
Two houses near the water, one condo
near downtown, professional photos,
dynamic pricing, smart locks, cleaners
on speed dial. His calendar looked full,
his revenue looked impressive, and his
friends treated him like he cracked the
code. Then 2025 rolled into 2026, and
the rules changed around him. Not
everywhere, but enough to make the
business unstable. A city meeting
introduced new registration
requirements. A neighbor filed
complaints about noise and parking.
Insurance renewals came back higher than
he expected. Cleaning costs jumped.
Platform fees felt heavier. Occupancy
became more seasonal, more volatile,
more sensitive to reviews and algorithm
shifts. Ryan was not losing money, but
he was losing control. and control is
the real asset. One night, after a guest
canled last minute and his cleaner still
charged him, Ryan opened his laptop and
ran a simple comparison. What would
happen if he stopped chasing weekends
and started chasing months? That was his
pivot into midterm rentals. Midterm
rentals sit in the space between a hotel
and a traditional lease. usually
furnished, usually utilities included,
usually stays measured in weeks or
months. The tenant profile is not the
bachelor party crowd. It is traveling
professionals, traveling nurses,
corporate relocation, insurance
displacement, families renovating their
homes, people in divorce transitions,
people waiting for a home purchase to
close. These tenants do not want a party
house. They want stability, privacy, a
kitchen, and reliable internet. They are
also willing to pay more than a typical
annual tenant because they are buying
flexibility and convenience. Ryan's
first midterm experiment was not
complicated. He took the condo near
downtown, removed the aggressive weekend
pricing, and listed it as a furnished
monthly stay. He targeted professionals.
He offered a clean, predictable package.
Furnished, utilities included, internet
included, one simple monthly rate, one
simple deposit, clear house rules, no
events, no parties, quiet hours, minimum
stay. The result surprised him. His
nightly rate was lower than peak Airbnb
weekends. But his vacancy dropped. His
turnover dropped even more. Instead of
constant cleaning, linen changes, and
key issues, he had one move in and one
move out every few months. fewer
problems, fewer messages, fewer
emergencies. His revenue became
smoother, his stress dropped. This is
why midterm rentals are outperforming
Airbnbs for many investors in 2026. It
is not because short-term rentals
stopped working. It is because midterm
rentals reduce fragility. Let me explain
fragility in plain language. A fragile
rental model breaks when one variable
changes. Regulations tighten. Insurance
spikes. Tourism dips. A platform changes
its algorithm. A new hotel opens nearby.
Reviews take a hit. If your entire
business depends on high occupancy at
high nightly rates with constant
turnover, you are operating a high
sensitivity machine. Mid-term rentals
absorb shocks better because the income
is contracted for longer periods. You
are not reselling the same nights over
and over. You are selling a block of
time to a tenant who values stability.
That changes the entire risk profile.
There is also a regulatory advantage.
Many cities that restrict short-term
rentals define them by length of stay.
That definition varies, but the pattern
is consistent. Longer stays are often
treated differently than nightly stays.
Midterm models are not a magic legal
loophole, and you still must comply with
local rules, but in many markets, they
are simply less controversial.
Neighborhoods fight party houses. They
do not fight a traveling nurse who parks
once and leaves in the morning. Ryan saw
another benefit immediately. Wear and
tear. An Airbnb can feel like a public
restaurant. Different people every few
days, different habits, different
respect levels. Midterm tenants are
living. They care more. They settle in.
They treat the place like a temporary
home, not a weekend playground. That
reduced Ryan's repair costs and extended
the life of his furnishings. But midterm
rentals are not passive. They require a
different operating system. Ryan had to
learn new fundamentals. Furnishing is
not decoration. Furnishing is product
design. You need durable couches, not
aesthetic couches. You need a real desk,
not a cute table. You need fast internet
that actually works. You need a kitchen
that can handle daily use. You need
simple, repeatable inventory. You need
backups. You need a process for
maintenance without disrupting the
tenants routine. He also had to learn
screening. Airbnb screening is reviews
and instant booking settings. Midterm
screening is closer to traditional
leasing. Income verification where
appropriate, background checks were
appropriate, clear lease terms, deposit
handling, identity confirmation. Ryan
built a simple screening flow and
stopped accepting tenants who felt
uncertain. In midterm, one bad tenant
can cost you months. So, you trade
quantity for quality. Pricing is another
difference. In short term, you win by
maximizing revenue per night. In
midterm, you win by maximizing revenue
per month while keeping vacancy low. The
pricing sweet spot is where your rate is
high enough to justify furnishing and
utilities, but fair enough that you
attract stable professionals who stay
longer. Ryan learned to stop competing
with Airbnbs and start competing with
furnished corporate housing and extended
stay options. His real competition was
not the party house down the street. It
was the furnished unit near the
hospital, the relocation apartment near
the corporate office, and the insurance
displacement inventory in the area. In
2026, the demand drivers for midterm
rentals have expanded beyond travel
nurses. Health care remains strong, but
corporate travel has evolved. Projects
run for months. Contract work has
increased. People relocate more
frequently. Life transitions are more
common. and housing transactions can
take longer in certain markets, creating
a natural gap where people need a
furnished place for a few months. Ryan's
second property conversion was one of
the houses. This time, he went further.
He designed it specifically for a
midterm tenant. A proper workspace,
blackout curtains, smart but simple,
durable floors, extra storage, a quiet,
calm vibe. He marketed it as a home for
professionals in transition, not as a
vacation destination. His average stay
length increased. His operational
workload dropped. Again, this is the
hidden truth. Mid-term rentals do not
always beat Airbnbs on peak revenue.
They often beat them on risk adjusted
returns. That is what sophisticated
investors care about. Not the highest
possible month, but the most stable
year. There are cons. You need more
capital upfront for furnishing. You must
understand local landlord tenant rules.
You need a strong lease. You need a plan
for utilities and maintenance. You need
to handle furniture depreciation. And
you need to accept that the growth is
quieter, not flashy. But Ryan did not
want flashy anymore. He wanted
predictable. By late 2026, his portfolio
looked different. One property remained
short-term because it still performed
well and the neighborhood supported it.
Two properties shifted to midterm. The
condo became his most stable cash
producer. His stress dropped. His
calendar stopped feeling like a daily
battle. He stopped managing constant
turnover and started managing a real
housing product. If you are an investor
listening to this, the takeaway is
simple. In 2026, smart real estate is
less about chasing the highest gross
revenue and more about building
resilient income streams. Midterm
rentals are outperforming Airbnbs for
many operators because they reduce
turnover, reduce platform dependence,
reduce regulatory friction in many
markets, and smooth cash flow. The right
move is not choosing one model forever.
The right move is building flexibility.
A property that can operate as
long-term, midterm, or short-term
depending on regulations and demand is a
powerful asset. Design your acquisition
and renovation decisions with that
flexibility in mind. Ryan did not become
a better investor because he found a new
hack. He became a better investor
because he traded volatility for
control. That is what savvy investors do
when the market shifts. They do not
complain. They adapt.

metadata.title: Understanding Security Deposits and Damage Waivers for Short-Term Rentals
metadata.author: Jacob and Elissa
metadata.shortDescription:
In this informative video, we dive deep into the crucial aspects of managing security deposits and damage waivers for your short-term rental properties on popular platforms like Airbnb, VRBO, and direct booking platforms. Whether you're a seasoned host or just starting out in the hospitality business, understanding the ins and outs of these financial safeguards is essential for a successful and stress-free hosting experience.

#ShortTermRentals #HostingTips #Airbnb #VRBO #DirectBookings #PropertyManagement

metadata.title: Security Deposit Alternatives
metadata.author: Nate Bunty
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video - Nate Bunty discusses an interesting trend in real estate investing. 

In order to enhance affordability, more security deposit alternatives are starting to come into the rental housing market. 

Rather than take a traditional 1x or 2x rents for a security deposit to cover skipped rent and damage to rental units, some landlords are offering a different approach. 

Most security deposit alternatives on the market today are guarantors or surety bond products. 

These products lower the initial costs for a tenant to get into a rental unit, but if a covered claim occurs the company providing the guarantee will look to collect damages from the tenant. 

Pure insurance solutions are starting to be released. 

Lease insurance provides a security deposit alternative that does not require the third party to collect from tenant in the event of a claim. 

Nate Bunty believes that lease insurance is the better solution because individual tenants don't need to qualify for the product AND insurance reduces friction between the property manager and tenant since the insurance doesn't have to collect damages from the tenant after the fact. 

If you would like more information about lease insurance - contact Nate Bunty - nate.bunty@assuredpartners.com or 717-481-3312

metadata.title: How Brian Biernat Scaled to 15+ Rentals with Rental Arbitrage | Quit His 6-Figure Job
metadata.author: Vicsmanor
metadata.shortDescription:
What does it take to leave a 28-year corporate career and build financial freedom through real estate?

In this episode of Vicsmanor, I sit down with Brian Biernat to break down how he and his wife scaled a furnished rental business using rental arbitrage (master leasing).

Brian explains how they started with wholesaling, discovered short-term rentals, and rapidly scaled to 15+ properties generating consistent cash flow, all before he eventually walked away from his six-figure telecom career.

In this interview, you’ll learn:
• How rental arbitrage works
• How Brian scaled from 0 to 15+ properties
• Why 2–3 bedroom rentals generate more cash flow

metadata.shortDescription:
Attend my free live rental arbitrage masterclass this week:
https://RichieMatthews.com

In this episode, you’ll learn how to fully automate your rental arbitrage business by hiring a virtual assistant, systemizing operations, and setting up tools and processes so it runs smoothly without you.

What You’ll Learn:
✅ How to build a fully automated rental arbitrage business that runs without you.
✅ The importance of focusing on systems and logistics instead of daily tasks.
✅ How to hire and train a virtual assistant to manage operations, guests, and turnovers.
✅ Tools and software to automate pricing, listings, and communication.
✅ How to scale from a few units to dozens while maintaining profitability.
✅ Ways to replace your income and gain true time freedom to live life on your terms.
✅ How to set up your team, test operations, and continuously optimize performance.
✅ The mindset shift from working in your business to working on your business.

Key Takeaways:
• You can run a profitable rental arbitrage business without being hands-on daily.
• Building systems and processes is the foundation of true automation.
• A well-trained virtual assistant can handle 90% of operations — from guest inquiries to turnovers.
• Using automation tools like Hospitable and PriceLabs streamlines communication and pricing.
• Partnering with reliable housekeepers and vendors keeps operations smooth.
• Focus on growth and scalability once your systems are in place.
• Freedom comes when your business runs without you — not because of you.

Tools Mentioned:
Hospitable
PriceLabs
AirDNA
CORT Furniture Rental
Google Sheets / Notion
Slack / WhatsApp
Turno (formerly TurnoverBnB)

This is the process to fully automate your rental arbitrage business—find profitable markets, hire a virtual assistant, use tools like Hospitable and PriceLabs, partner with furniture rental companies, and build systems so your business runs smoothly without you.

0:00 – Introduction: How to Automate Your Business

11:31 - Final Thoughts / Freedom Mindset

Today I had the honor of speaking with Farhan Abbasi. Farhan is based out of Boston Massachusetts and runs a coworking space called Coalition Downtown while also managing a portfolio of 15 properties also located in the Boston area.

Farhan has been in the rental arbitrage subleasing space since 2012 and throughout his short term rental ventures managed 40 properties but has had to scale back to due to tightening regulations.

metadata.title: The Six-Figure Airbnb Arbitrage System Without Owning Property
metadata.author: Linda Kim
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to build passive income without owning property?

In this episode, I break down Airbnb rental arbitrage step by step, from finding the right market and pitching landlords to furnishing your first unit and scaling your business.

After leaving my corporate career, I took a chance on Airbnb rental arbitrage with zero experience. That decision led to a six-figure business, and in this episode, I share the exact process, the mistakes I made, and the lessons I wish I'd known from the start.

You'll learn how to:

✅ Find profitable markets using real data
✅ Approach landlords with confidence
✅ Budget and furnish your first Airbnb
✅ Automate your business with systems and virtual assistants
✅ Scale without owning a single property

If you've been looking for a realistic path to building income and creating more freedom, this episode is for you.

Subscribe for more conversations on entrepreneurship, passive income, and building a business that gives you more freedom.

#Airbnb #AirbnbArbitrage #AirbnbBusiness #ShortTermRentals #Entrepreneurship #PassiveIncome #FinancialFreedom

GUESTS BIO
Brian Fontenot - is a Real Estate Investor, Philanthropist, Public Speaker, World Traveler, and Short Term Rental Arbitrage Operator with 20+ units in the Houston area. 
 
HIGHLIGHTS OF THE EPISODE
03:59  Brian’s biography/introduction
05:10  How Brian started and what led him on this path.
06:24  What convinced Brian to quit his 9-5 job and start his STR business.
08:43  How Brian got into his 1st deal.
10:18  What Brian did to acquire his 1st rental property.
11:11  What Brian and his team are focused on for their STR business.
12:43  How Brian identifies what the vacancies look like when looking for a property.

25:41  What he does in his business now.
27:52  How he finds investors and what he offers to find potential investors.
30:06  Raises money and gets investors on for arbitrage.
32:27  How they pivot and learned on the heat of Covid. 
36:09  Providing value to the people we want to serve.
37:09  Are they pivoting to a week-long stay or just with shorter-term stays.
38:30  Looking at International properties.
39:39  Brian’s goals and vision for the business.
42:06  Where can people get in touch with Brian.
42:57  Brian’s #1 secret to success in short term rentals.

NOTABLE QUOTES (KEY LESSONS):

"Take the leap. There's nothing holding you back." - Brian Fontenot

"Just the ability to be able to work from anywhere. People don't take it lightly but I think people now see the beauty of it and now people are more flexible about going to different places and where they stay and such." - Brian Fontenot

"We just want to be positioned to be able to offer every possible option that people could look to so that we can be able to make the most with our costumers." - Brian Fontenot

"As long as you anticipate the people's needs that you serve, you will find success to highest degree." - Brian Fontenot

metadata.shortDescription:
How to make money with Airbnb without owning property using fractional hosting instead of rental arbitrage.

🔴 Learn the Airbnb fundamentals with my FREE course ➡️ https://www.skool.com/myfirstbnb/about

🎬 Watch Next: Airbnb Changed Their Algorithm — https://youtu.be/AYUyx6udg7M?si=JyYX6aq_FSJGHsJs

===========================
Connect with us!

YouTube: ➡︎ @quentinwestofficial 
Instagram: ➡︎ @quentinwestofficial
TikTok: ➡︎ @quentinwestofficial

===========================
Here are the ways to work with us:

⚡️ Start with the FREE course: ➡︎ https://www.skool.com/myfirstbnb/about

#AirbnbBusiness #FractionalHosting #AirbnbArbitrage #ShortTermRentals

Can you make money with Airbnb without owning property? Absolutely — but rental arbitrage isn’t the only way to do it.

I built an Airbnb arbitrage business to 47 units across three states and well over six figures a month in revenue. But scaling that business also meant leases, furniture, debt, cleaning crews, maintenance, fixed expenses, and thousands of dollars invested into each new property. After experiencing the downside of that leverage firsthand, I started looking for a lower-overhead way to build Airbnb cash flow.

That led me to fractional hosting: partnering with existing Airbnb owners to improve their listing, pricing, marketing, guest experience, and revenue without leasing or owning the property yourself. In this video, I break down how fractional hosting works, how it differs from Airbnb arbitrage and traditional cohosting, why an owner would pay for it, and the economics behind the model — including the 18.68% average revenue increase we’ve measured across hosts we’ve worked with.

In this video, you’ll learn:
• How to Airbnb without owning property
• Why I moved away from rental arbitrage after scaling to 47 units
• What fractional hosting is and how the business model works
• How fractional hosting differs from traditional Airbnb cohosting
• Why high-occupancy Airbnb listings can signal a revenue opportunity
• How a 15% revenue-share model can work for both you and the property owner
• Why lower overhead can make this model easier to scale
• Who fractional hosting is — and is not — a good fit for
• The real skills you need to start building an Airbnb revenue management business

Fractional hosting isn’t passive income, and it isn’t a shortcut to getting rich. You still have to learn Airbnb pricing and revenue strategy, prospect for owners, have sales conversations, build relationships, and develop a track record. But unlike rental arbitrage, you don’t need to take on a new lease, furnish another property, or add major fixed expenses every time you grow.

If you want to learn what makes an Airbnb property perform, which markets and properties to look for, and how to find owners who may be open to working with you, grab the free course here:

🔴 https://www.skool.com/myfirstbnb/about

Our mission  is to help Airbnb entrepreneurs build profitable, sustainable businesses while developing the skills and cash flow that can create more freedom and opportunity.

Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only. Revenue figures, examples, and past results do not guarantee future performance. Business and real estate results vary based on market conditions, experience, execution, property characteristics, and other factors.

metadata.shortDescription:
What if you could build a six-figure income in real estate without ever buying a single property, getting a mortgage, or putting up hundreds of thousands of dollars? That is exactly what Colin Wright has done, and in this episode of the Official Success Formula, he breaks down every single step of the Airbnb arbitrage model that took him from a garbage man and furniture mover in Canada to controlling nearly 200 Airbnb units and generating $600,000 a month in revenue in the United States.

Colin shares how he stumbled onto the short-term rental arbitrage model in 2022 when he was looking for a way to legally immigrate to the US on an E2 investor visa. What started as a single three-bedroom house in Austin, Texas, which still makes him $2,000 to $2,500 in net profit every single month, turned into one of the most impressive Airbnb portfolios in North America. And the best part? He did it without ever owning a single piece of real estate in America.

In this episode, you will learn how to find landlords willing to let you sublet their property on Airbnb, the exact tools Colin uses to analyze markets and predict profitability before signing a lease, why starting with a studio or one-bedroom apartment is almost always the smartest move for beginners, how to negotiate free rent concessions and lower security deposits, the full tech stack including Price Labs, Hospitable, smart locks, and noise sensors that makes his operation nearly passive, and how the E2 investor visa works and why Airbnb arbitrage is one of the most viable legal pathways to moving to the United States.

Whether you are a complete beginner looking for a low-risk entry point into real estate, a business owner exploring passive income streams, or someone outside the US looking for a legal and profitable way to immigrate, this episode is genuinely one of the most valuable conversations we have ever had on the show.

Attend my upcoming free live rental arbitrage workshop:
https://RichieMatthews.com

In this episode, I’m breaking down the real amount of time it takes to start and run an apartment arbitrage business — even with a full-time job and family. You’ll see exactly how I scaled to 62 properties in under three years working just 30 minutes per day once systemized.

What You’ll Learn:
✅ How I launched my first arbitrage unit while working full-time
✅ My daily time commitment for market research and acquisitions
✅ The step-by-step process I use to close a deal in 6–8 weeks
✅ Why you should never self-manage or hire a property manager
✅ How to automate 90% of operations with a $4/hour VA, and software
✅ Why apartment arbitrage is inherently scalable (and how to scale it)

Key Takeaways:
• Market research: 15–20 minutes per day for 1–2 weeks
• Acquisitions: 15–30 minutes per day until you land a deal
• After setup: ~30 minutes per day with VA handling 90% of tasks
• Scaled from 18 units to 35 units in six months by systemizing

Tools Mentioned:
Virtual Assistants (our VA protocol)
Publicly available STR software for automation
AirDNA for market research
Zillow + HotPads for acquisitions

This is the exact process I used to scale my rental arbitrage portfolio from 1 property to 62 without sacrificing my family time — no guesswork, just systems.

5:04 – 30 minutes per day is all it takes
5:19 – Scaling to 46+ properties in 24 months
5:33 – Mistakes I made before automating
6:13 – Final thoughts — systemize & scale

metadata.title: Billion Dollar Blueprint For Apartment Arbitrage
metadata.author: Richie Matthews
metadata.shortDescription:
Attend my free live rental arbitrage masterclass this week:
https://RichieMatthews.com

In this episode, we break down how a scalable rental arbitrage system helped grow from 18 to 35 units in just six months—running only 30 minutes a day through full automation and smart business systems.

What You’ll Learn:
✅ How to scale a rental arbitrage business from 18 to 35 units in just 6 months
✅ The system that lets you manage everything in only 30 minutes a day
✅ How to fully automate your operations and step out of daily management
✅ Why a scalable business model beats traditional real estate investing
✅ How to build a side hustle that can replace (or supplement) your income
✅ Tips for balancing business growth while keeping your time freedom

Key Takeaways:
• Scalability is everything — build a model that grows unit by unit using cash flow, not constant reinvestment.
• Automation = freedom — with the right systems and VAs, you can run your business in just 30 minutes a day.
• Growth over perfection — even if margins shrink slightly, scaling doubles your total income.
• Systemize early — create processes and tech tools that remove you from day-to-day operations.
• Rental arbitrage is flexible — it works whether you want to replace your income or build a part-time side hustle.

Tools Mentioned:
AirDNA
Rentometer
Hospitable
PriceLabs
Channel Manager
Virtual Assistants (VAs)
SOPs/Protocols System
CORT Furniture Rental

This is the process: identify profitable markets using data tools like AirDNA and Rentometer, secure legal and high-demand properties, list them across multiple platforms, automate operations with a VA and tools like Hospitable and PriceLabs, and scale unit by unit through cash flow reinvestment.

Timestamps:
0:00 – Introduction: How to Systemize Your Business
1:12 – The Power of Scalable Models like Rental Arbitrage
1:38 – 4 Basics Steps in Rental Arbitrage
4:28 – Following Corporate Leases Explained
7:25 – Followed Sonder's Marketing Strategy
9:42 – How I Followed Sonder’s Strategy to Scale Fast
11:20 - Verifying and Assessing Markets
14:18 - Understanding the New Supply and Demand Shift in Cities
15:48 - Systemizing the Business
18:24 - How I Started My First Rental Unit
19:22 - Scaling a Rental Arbitrage Business Using the Sonder's Model
21:22 - Closing Thoughts: Build, Automate, and Scale

#rentalarbitrage  #airbnbbusiness  #realestate  #passiveincome  #propertyinvestment  #shorttermrental  #realestateinvesting  #entrepreneur  #airbnbhost  #apartmentarbitrage  #scale  

Like this video if it helped you understand the time commitment of rental arbitrage better, and subscribe for more real estate investing content!

The video discusses how to maximize profits through rental arbitrage on platforms such as Airbnb and VRBO. The host interviews guest Quentin West, who quickly scaled his Airbnb business, earning over $100,000 per month in gross revenue within 24 months. West initially entered the short-term rental space out of necessity when he couldn't keep up with his mortgage payments after becoming a full-time real estate agent. He stumbled upon the Airbnb arbitrage model, where he rented properties and subleased them on Airbnb, allowing him to make several thousand dollars a month in profit off a property. West recommends using a channel manager to sync calendars between Airbnb and VRBO. He also suggests starting with arbitrage, wholesaling, or flipping to create cash flow, as opposed to buying rentals. West now coaches others on how to succeed in the short-term rental space, including how to build a business entity and business credit to leverage for financing. Finally, the video touches on the importance of building relationships with property owners and guests, providing value, and avoiding common mistakes like not conducting inspections or overthinking the process.

In this episode of The Landlord Diaries, we sit down with mid-term rental expert, William Dotson, who specializes in insurance housing hosting families that have been displaced from a disaster. His level of hospitality, expertise & heart for the guest(s) is contagious. At this time, Will's portfolio is all mid-term rentals. He operates around 10 locally in Nashville & 2 out of state. With over 12 properties under his management and more in development, William has become a master at leveraging partnerships with Furnished Finder hosts and navigating the complexities of MTR insurance housing. Will has turned disaster displacement into opportunity, offering much-needed housing while expanding his business. Join us as Will discusses his journey from launching his first mid-term rental to scaling his portfolio across Nashville, California, and Washington, all while building a successful strategy around insurance contracts.

Throughout the episode, William walks us through his booking process, the importance of understanding ALE coverage, and his partnership strategies that allow him to expand his network. With actionable tips on marketing, property management, and contracts, this conversation is a treasure trove of insights for real estate investors aiming to dive into the mid-term rental market.

Tune in for expert advice on property management, building partnerships, insurance intricacies, and tips on successfully managing properties across state lines.

metadata.title: Rent Can't Go Up? Here's the Midterm Rental Alternative That Pays
metadata.author: John Racine
metadata.shortDescription:
https://cjrstays.com
Get you FREE Property Projection at https://cjrstays.com/book

If your insurance, taxes, and maintenance keep going up but the market won't let you raise rent — you're asking how to survive. 

What if you're asking the wrong question?

I was at a CFRI (Central Florida Realty Investors) landlord panel recently, and nobody mentioned midterm rentals. In this video I break down why a furnished midterm rental — 30 days to 6 months for traveling nurses, corporate relocations, insurance stays, and construction crews — can generate more revenue from the same property, and the exact math you need to run before you switch.

You'll see:
• Why traditional long-term rentals get squeezed when expenses rise
• What a midterm rental actually is (and how it's different from Airbnb)
• Who pays the premium — and why it's not always the tenant
• $2,000 long-term vs $3,000 and $3,500 midterm at 85% occupancy
• Furnishing costs, vacancy, and simple payback period
• How to research your market on Furnished Finder and Airbnb

This is not a forecast and not financial advice. Run your own numbers for your market, check your local ordinances and HOA rules, and model lower occupancy before you decide.Got a rental you're struggling to raise rent on? Comment what market you're in and I'll tell you what I'd research first.— John Racine, CJR Stays

0:00 The Question Every Landlord Is Asking
1:37 Why Rental Expenses Keep Squeezing Cash Flow
3:06 What a Midterm Rental Actually Is
4:45 Who Pays the Premium (And Why)
6:24 The $2,000 vs $3,000 Math
8:24 What If It's $3,500 a Month?
8:54 Furnishing Costs and Payback
9:37 Vacancy: The Hidden Cost to Compare
10:25 My CJR Stays Arbitrage Example
11:14 How to Research Your Market (Furnished Finder + Airbnb)

videos.full_text: I was at a real estate investors meeting here in Central Florida recently and something happened that really got me thinking. The meeting was hosted by CFRI, the Central Florida Realty Investors Association, and the main presentation was a panel discussion about landlording tips and strategies. And there were some very experienced people on that panel. There was a professional property manager, someone specializing in student housing, an investor with multiple single-family rentals, a couple of short-term rentals, and even a condo hotel. So it was a very diverse group with very different perspectives on rental property investing. One of the questions asked was a question that I think a lot of landlords are struggling with right now. And essentially that question was, what do you do when your expenses keep increasing, things like property taxes, insurance, maintenance, but the rental market won't support raising your rent? Now that's a great question. And the panelists offered several suggestions based on their experiences. But as I listened to the responses, something really struck me. Nobody mentioned what I believe could be one of the most interesting alternatives that is available to rental property investors, mid-term rentals. And I kept thinking, what if we are asking the wrong question? Instead of asking how we can survive increasing expenses when rents aren't keeping pace, shouldn't we be asking how we can generate more revenue from the property that we already have? Because sometimes the problem isn't the property, sometimes the problem is the rental strategy. And today I want to show you why mid-term rentals might be an option that's worth exploring, not necessarily as a permanent replacement for traditional rentals, but potentially as a bridge until market conditions improve. And I'm going to walk you through the numbers because this is one of those strategies where the math really matters. Now let's start with something we can probably all agree on. Owning rental property has become more expensive. Insurance premiums can increase significantly, property taxes can go up, maintenance costs certainly aren't getting any cheaper. And depending on your market, you may not have the ability to increase rents enough to offset those expenses. So what happens? Your cash flow gets squeezed. And when investors start talking about solutions, conversation often revolves around a few familiar ideas. Can I reduce expenses? Can I negotiate a better insurance premium? Can I increase the rent? Can I make improvements that justify charging more? And these are all perfectly reasonable questions, but there's another question that I think deserves just as much attention. Am I using the most appropriate rental strategy for this property in this market at this particular time? Think about that for a second. As real estate investors, we spend a tremendous amount of time analyzing properties before we purchase them. We look at acquisition costs, financing, cash flow, cap rates, cash on cash returns, and potential appreciation. But how often do we revisit the actual rental strategy after we've owned the property for a few years? We buy a single-family home, we rent it to someone on a 12-month lease, and then we continue doing that year after year. But what happens when the economics change? Shouldn't we reconsider that strategy? I'm not suggesting there's anything wrong with traditional long-term rentals. They're an excellent investment strategy in the right circumstances, but they're not necessarily the only strategy available for that property. This brings me to mid-term rentals. If you're unfamiliar with the term, a mid-term rental or MTR is generally a furnished rental designed for people who need accommodations for 30 days or longer. Some stays might be 30 days, some might be 60, 90, or even 6 months. And here's why I find this strategy particularly interesting for traditional landlords. You're not necessarily trying to turn your property into a vacation rental. You're not necessarily dealing with new guests every 3 or 4 days. You're provided furnished housing to people who need somewhere to live temporarily. In many respects, it can operate similarly to a traditional rental. You can have a written lease agreement, you can collect a security deposit where it's permitted, you can establish utility allowances and provisions for excessive usage, you can outline cleaning responsibilities, maintenance expectations, and property rules. And because your tenants are generally staying longer than typical vacation rental guests, you're not necessarily dealing with the same frequency of turnovers. Now, there are additional responsibilities. You're furnishing the property. You're typically providing utilities and internet. You may have more frequent tenant transitions than with a traditional 12-month lease, but those differences can be manageable. And here's something else worth considering. Depending on your location, local regulations, and HOA requirements, a mid-term rental may be permitted where short-term vacation rentals are restricted. Now, that's not universal, and you absolutely need to verify the rules for your particular property, but it can create opportunities that aren't available to traditional short-term rental operators. And the potential benefit? You may be able to generate substantially more monthly rental revenue than you would with an unfurnished traditional long-term lease. But why would someone pay that premium? That brings us to the customer. When I talk to investors about mid-term rentals, one of the first things that comes up is traveling nurses. And yes, traveling healthcare professionals are certainly one potential customer segment, but they're far from the only one. Let's say someone's home suffers significant water damage or a fire. Their insurance company may need to arrange temporary housing for the family while repairs are being completed. The family might need somewhere to live for three, four, six months or longer, and they're probably not looking for an unfurnished apartment where they need to purchase furniture, establish utilities, and sign a 12-month lease. They need somewhere they can move into immediately. Or consider corporate relocations. A company transfers an employee to a new market. That employee needs somewhere to stay for 60 or 90 days while they find permanent housing. What about traveling executives? Construction crews working on major infrastructure projects. Employees brought into town temporarily by a large local employer. People who have sold their homes but haven't closed on their next property. There are numerous reasons someone might need furnished housing for just a few months. And here's what makes this particularly interesting. Some of these customers aren't paying for the housing themselves. Their employer may be paying. Their insurance company may be covering the expense. A corporate relocation provider may be arranging accommodations. Now, that doesn't mean price is irrelevant. These organizations have budgets, policies, and financial expectations, but the customer isn't necessarily comparing your furnished property to the cheapest available 12 month apartment lease. They're comparing it to other temporary housing solutions, and that's a very different market. So, when we talk about increasing rental revenue, we're not necessarily talking about charging your existing tenant more money. talking about serving a completely different customer with different housing needs, and that's an important distinction. Now, let's get into the financial side because this is where things become interesting. Let's imagine you own a three bedroom, two bath single family rental. You're currently renting it for $2,000 per month, so that's $24,000 per year in potential gross rental income, assuming that the property stays occupied for all 12 months. But your insurance premium increases, your property taxes increase, and suddenly you're making $300 less per month than you were previously. That's $3,600 per year in additional expenses. And let's say the traditional rental market won't support raising the rent. So, what are your options? You could absorb the additional expense, you could try to reduce costs elsewhere, or you could investigate whether the property might perform better as a furnished mid-term rental. Let's say you start researching your market and find comparable furnished properties advertised for around $3,000 per month. Now, that's not proof that you'll receive $7,000. An advertised rate isn't the same as actual collected revenue, but it gives you a starting point for further research. Let's build a hypothetical example. Traditional long-term rental, monthly rent $2,000. Annual potential rental revenue, $24,000. Now, let's look at a potential mid-term rental scenario. Monthly advertised rate $3,000. But instead of assuming 100% occupancy, let's use 85% economic occupancy for our illustration. That gives us approximately $30,600 in annual rental revenue. Already we're looking at $6,600 more in annual gross revenue, but we're not finished because we have additional operating expenses. Let's estimate $300 per month for utilities and internet. That's $3,600 annually. Let's assume another $1,200 per year in incremental cleaning supplies and additional maintenance. Now our incremental operating expenses total $4,800. So, the additional annual operating income compared with the fully long-term rental example is approximately $1,800. That's before accounting for furnishing costs, financing, taxes, and any other differences we haven't modeled. And suddenly that additional $1,000 in advertised monthly rent doesn't look quite as impressive now, does it? That's exactly why you have to run the numbers. But now consider a very different scenario. What if your research suggests the property could realistically come in $3,500 a month? Using that same 85% economic occupancy assumption, you're looking at $35,700 in annual revenue. Subtract the same $4,800 in additional operating expenses, that leaves approximately $30,900 compared with the $24,000 traditional rental. That's an additional $6,900 annually. Now we're talking about a potentially meaningful difference, but there is another expense that we haven't discussed, furniture, fixtures, and equipment. One of the biggest differences between a long-term rental and a mid-term rental is that your property needs to be furnished, beds, mattresses, sofas, dining furniture, kitchen equipment, televisions, linen, and everything else somebody needs to move in comfortably. And that's going to require an investment. Let's say you spend $6,000 furnishing and equipping the property. Using our second example where the mid-term rental generates approximately $6,900 in additional annual operating income, your simple payback period would be a little over 10 months. That's potentially attractive, but remember this is an illustration, it's not a forecast. If your occupancy drops, your furnishing costs are higher, or your operating expenses exceed expectations, your payback period gets longer. Here's where I want to connect this back to something that came up at the CFRI meeting. There was discussion about the financial impact of having a rental property sit vacant for a month or two. Let's use that same $2,000 per month property. If it sits vacant for two months, you've lost $4,000 in potential revenue. Now I'm not suggesting you can automatically take that $4,000 and use it to furnish the property. Lost revenue is not available cash, and converting to a mid-term rental can create its own vacancy period. But shouldn't we at least consider and compare the financial consequences of those different options? If you're already facing a vacancy, could that be an opportunity to reposition the property? Could you invest in furnishing it and potentially generate additional income over the next 12 or 24 months? Maybe, maybe not, but you won't know until you run the numbers. And that's really my point. Let me give you a quick example from my own experience. Through CGR Stays, my property management, co-hosting and furnished rental business, we operate a rental arbitrage property. For those unfamiliar with rental arbitrage, we're leasing the property from the owner and then operating it as a furnished rental with the appropriate permissions. Our monthly rent obligation is $3,000. And through our furnished rental operations, we've been able to generate rental revenue that is significantly above that amount. Now, I'm not going to suggest that every property can achieve those results, and revenue is not profit. We still have utilities, operating expenses, maintenance, furnishing costs, and other obligations. But my point is that the property's income potential isn't necessarily limited to what someone would pay under a traditional 12-month unfurnished lease. Different rental strategies can create different revenue opportunities, and that's something I've seen firsthand. So what should you do if you're a landlord watching and you're wondering whether mid-term rentals might work for your property? I start with some basic research. And you don't have to become an expert overnight. First, take a look at Furnished Finder. It's a platform focused on furnished monthly rentals. Search your market. Look for properties comparable to yours. What are they asking per month? How are they furnished? What amenities are included? What types of properties are being advertised? Next, look over at Airbnb. And don't just look at weekend vacation rentals. Explore longer stays and monthly pricing. See what furnished properties are being offered for in your area. Now, neither platform tells you everything you need to know. Listings don't automatically reveal actual occupancy, achieve rental revenue, or even profitability, but they can help you identify whether there's an opportunity worth investigating. Then start thinking about demand. Are there major hospitals nearby, large employers, corporate offices, construction projects, relocation activity? Is there a reason someone would need temporary furnished housing in your particular market? And then, of course, verify the regulations. Check your local ordinances, review your HOA or condominium restrictions. Make sure you understand the rules governing rental durations and furnished housing. And finally, run the numbers. Compare your current rental strategy against a realistic mid-term rental scenario. Include the furnishing investment, include utilities, include vacancy, include maintenance, management, cleaning, and other operating costs. And don't just calculate the best-case scenario. Look at what happens if occupancy is lower than expected because a strategy that looks fantastic at 95% occupancy might not make sense at 65%. You need to understand both the opportunity and the risk. Thank you so much for watching. We'll see you in the next video.

metadata.title: What is Lessors Risk or Commercial Landlord Insurance, and What Does it Cover?
metadata.author: Elemental Risk Management
metadata.shortDescription:
Lessor's risk insurance (LRO), also known as landlord insurance, is a policy intended to protect the owner of a commercial building rented to other people. Landlords shall be responsible legally for any damage to their property. In addition, the house should be covered from fire, vandalism, or other damage. A lesson's risk policy accounts for the benefit of the landowner both for general liability and property insurance.

Insurance and welcome to the next video
