liability coverage that's within your
renter's policy.
What is personal liability coverage?
Personal liability insurance will
protect you from any damages or injuries
that someone else sustains and they deem
you responsible for those.
What are some scenarios that might
occur?
So say you're sitting out in the front
yard with your dog. Someone walks by the
house and the dog barks. It startles the
individual and maybe they fall down and
have an injury. They might hold you
responsible for that.
Another situation is your child's in the
backyard throwing a ball around.
And that ball then goes through the
neighbor's window causing some damages.
Again, they would probably hold you
responsible.
The third scenario is you leave the
bathroom sink running all day while
you're at work. The water overflows,
goes into the unit below you causing
damage. The landlord potentially could
come after you for those damages.
In all three scenarios, a personal
liability policy will protect you from
paying out-of-pocket costs.
This is just another reason why the low
cost of a renter's policy really can
help reduce your risk and potentially
save you money over the long run.
If you have any questions about what

not cover, please feel free to reach out
to us. And if you know anyone who's a

somewhere else if you got displaced from

disaster.

you enjoy the videos.

metadata.title: Lessor's Risk Only (LRO) - Landlord Insurance & Commercial Buildings
metadata.author: CID Insurance
metadata.shortDescription:
Do you write Lessor's Risk policies or Landlord Insurance? Learn how to recognize and understand the different types of commercial buildings, learn about the underwriting guidelines that need to be considered and gain more knowledge about property components and how to insure them. Our team will teach you the secrets to a fast, quotable submission and about the latest industry changes and trends.

Timestamps:

00:00 Start
02:47 Lessor's Risk Only Definition
04:02 Types of Lessor's Risk Buildings
07:40 Underwriting Characteristics to Consider
14:43 Building Property Valuation
19:46 Lessor's Risk Coverages
24:26 LRO Submissions & Quotes

Lessors Risk Definition

Lessor's Risk Only (LRO): provides liability and property coverage for building owners who lease out their entire building; or the building owner occupies a portion of the building and leases out the remainder of the building (Provides coverage for the landlord)

Types of Lessors Risk Buildings:

Professional Buildings – medical offices, professional offices, etc.
Commercial Buildings – warehouses, light mfg., garage businesses, etc.
Mixed Use Buildings – occupied by both commercial and residential tenants
Retail Strip Malls – mercantile businesses, restaurants, etc.
Business Park Associations – Condominiums or PUDs

Underwriting Characteristics to Consider:

Type of Tenant Occupancy
Any vacancies?
Building Characteristics:
-Age of the building
-Building updates
-Maintenance, condition and location of the building
-Number of stories/size of the building
-Sprinklered?

Building Property Valuation:

Building Replacement Cost will vary by:
-State location  
-Construction type
-Building height/square footage/age
-Building quality
Building construction cost per square foot will vary by structure use
Building valuation = cost per square foot x total square footage

Lessors Risk Coverages:

Property – Building & other property components
Business Income – Loss of Rents
Building Ordinance – Coverages A, B & C available
Equipment Breakdown
Property Enhancement Endorsement
General Liability
Hired & Non-Owned Auto Liability

Lessors Risk Submissions:

Acord 125, 126 & 140 – include building square footage, tenants, annual rents
Supplemental – We can quote off most carrier’s applications or our LRO supplemental is available on our website
Rent Roll/Tenant List
Statement of Values – if applicable
3-5 Years Loss Runs – We can quote subject to clean loss history
Target Premium

Send your submissions to submissions@cidinsurance.com

--

Learn More About CID:
Our Website: https://www.cidinsurance.com/
Get a Quote: https://www.cidinsurance.com/submit-for-quote/
Get Appointed: https://www.cidinsurance.com/contact/become-a-producer/
Register for Webinars: https://www.cidinsurance.com/resources/webinars/

CID Insurance Programs is an E&S Wholesaler specializing in commercial insurance products designed for independent and captive insurance brokers’ business client’s needs.

Our wholesale business insurance products encompass a broad range of preferred to manageable hard-to-place risks.  CID Insurance has developed strong relationships with both admitted and non-admitted markets.  Our commitment is to make the quote and bind process fast and easy for our retail insurance brokers.

metadata.shortDescription:
👉 Access our Airbnb Masterclass ➜ https://bit.ly/VRMMasterclass

In this episode of the VRM podcast, Jon Bell and Julian Sage demystify the hottest investment strategies—Rental Arbitrage, Cohosting, BRRRR, and Turnkey—and explain how each model works and which might be right for your goals.

You’ll learn how to:

Understand Rental Arbitrage: Lease properties long-term and relist them on Airbnb for profit—no down payment required and fast to launch.

Dive into Cohosting: Partner with owners to manage their listings for a share of revenue—leveraging your expertise without owning any real estate.

Master the BRRRR method: Buy, Rehab, Rent, Refinance, Repeat—how to recycle capital into new acquisitions and build a portfolio with minimal cash outlay.

Explore Turnkey investing: Purchase fully managed properties from specialized operators and step into immediate cash flow—trading upfront convenience for slightly lower cap rates.

Compare the differences: Key metrics on cash requirements, risk profiles, control levels, and scalability so you can choose the path that fits your appetite and timeline.

By the end of this episode, you’ll have a clear side-by-side playbook of these four strategies—empowering you to decide how to enter, scale, or diversify your short-term rental business.

metadata.author: Short Term Sage - Airbnb, Vacation Rental Host
metadata.shortDescription:
👉 Access our Airbnb Masterclass ➜ https://bit.ly/VRMMasterclass

In this video, Jon Bell and Julian Sage explore the key challenges and trade-offs between Rental Arbitrage and Cohosting—so you can decide which model aligns best with your goals and resources.

You’ll learn how to:

Define business models: Understand the core differences—leasing-to-rent versus managing owner properties—and what each approach demands in time, capital, and risk.

Assess startup costs & cash flow: Compare up-front requirements (deposits, furnishing) for arbitrage against minimal capital but slimmer margins in cohosting.

Evaluate operational control: See how full autonomy over pricing and rules in arbitrage stacks up against the relationship-driven nature and owner approvals in cohosting.

Manage landlord relationships: Learn negotiation tactics for securing lease terms in arbitrage versus building trust and service agreements with property owners in cohosting.

Scale strategically: Identify which model offers faster growth potential—bulk-leasing multiple units versus adding cohosted properties with lower overhead.

By the end of this video, you’ll have a clear framework to choose—or blend—Rental Arbitrage and Cohosting strategies to optimize profit, minimize headaches, and grow your Airbnb business.

🚀 Watch our free training to start your own Airbnb Management Business: http://bnbfastlane.com/ftyt

There are 3 ways to build an Airbnb business - Co-Hosting, Rental Arbitrage, and Property Management. Most people pick the wrong one and wonder why they can't scale. 

We went from zero to managing 60+ properties and $2.5 million in Airbnb booking revenue in 2023 using one specific model - and in this video we break down exactly why it beats the other two and how to know which one is right for your situation.

What you'll learn in this video:
✅ The key differences between co-hosting, rental arbitrage and property management - and the pros and cons of each 
✅ Why rental arbitrage has been done to death by YouTube gurus for nearly a decade - and the risks most people don't talk about 
✅ Why co-hosting limits your ability to scale and why it's harder to build a sellable business with this model 
✅ How the property management model allowed us to go from zero to 60+ properties without signing a single lease 
✅ The ideal client avatar that made our Gold Coast business work - and how to find the same type of client in your market 
✅ How to decide which model is actually right for your specific situation and market

🎯 Book a free strategy session with Aaron & Nathan - we'll answer your questions and map out the exact launch plan for your specific market, completely free: https://bnbfastlane.com/ftyt

Join our free community of Airbnb entrepreneurs: https://www.facebook.com/share/g/19e8fhRxo3/
Questions? Email us: hello@bnbfastlane.com

About Aaron & Nathan - BNB Fastlane
We're two entrepreneurs who built and sold a 60+ property Airbnb Management Business in under 2 years - no prior experience, no funding, and without signing a single rental lease. Operating from the Gold Coast, Australia's most competitive short-term rental market, we consistently outperformed comparable properties by 30-75% in earnings. Airbnb Superhosts, Booking.com Preferred Partners, and one of Australia's first Marriott Homes & Villas partners - we founded BNB Fastlane to give you the exact playbook we used.

metadata.title: The Insurance Housing Blueprint Generating 4x Market Rate Returns w/ Ruben Kanya | Ep. 114
metadata.author: Landlord Diaries - The Monthly Rentals Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to The Landlord Diaries! In this episode, we dive deep into the profitable niche of mid-term rental insurance with real estate expert Ruben Kanya @therealestateexperiment. With over a decade of experience and a portfolio controlling over 30 homes, Ruben reveals how he rents homes to families displaced by disasters at 4x the long-term market rate. From building a real estate portfolio to navigating insurance housing, Ruben shares game-changing strategies to optimize for mid-term rentals in today’s tight housing market.

Learn how Ruben’s buy box strategy helps him secure 4-5 bedroom homes, perfect for displaced families, and how data-driven decisions in mid-term rentals can significantly boost your ROI. Ruben’s “napkin math” example shows a displaced family in his area of Atlanta, GA, would likely have $86,000 available for housing which breaks down to $7,166/month for 12 months. (Catch this part of the conversation at 45 minutes.)

If you’re a real estate investor looking to maximize your rental income, leverage insurance contracts, and avoid common mistakes, tune in now!

In this episode we cover:
0:00 Intro- Welcome to The Landlord Diaries
3:50 The exciting mid-term rental insurance space
7:45 Hosting someone through disaster
9:10 Ruben’s buy box or real estate purchasing strategy
10:50 Don’t be a penny wise & a dollar foolish with tenant requests
11:55 There are SO MANY ways you can take a mid-term rental
13:30 Insurance housing is more prevalent than you might think
13:45 Understand your insurance rights: It’s in your best interest to call your public adjuster first before your insurance company
15:45 The Invested Escapes Portfolio & Mastermind Training Program
17:30 Embracing market shortages with 4-5 bedroom homes
18:15 Imagine hotel life for a family of 5 with 2 dogs…
19:45 Half of the Furnished Finder supply is studios or one bedrooms
20:30 Data is all relative, do the math & see the value in midterm rentals
22:00 Katie’s wine bottle analogy
22:35 Katie’s jump from 10-14 properties in months
24:25 The insurance corporate housing blueprint
29:05 Relocation specialists swipe quickly through Furnished Finder
30:35 STR/Airbnb hosts optimize for experience, MTR hosts optimize for functionality 
32:25 Midterm rentals are an art, not a science. Brag about your functional amenities. 
33:45 Optimize for Midterm Rentals: 30 day notice to vacate & fill gaps with short term
37:25 When the STR/MTR hybrid strategy fails
38:35 National Gross Housing Margin: The calculated formula insurance companies use
39:45 Know Insurance Terms For Gross Profit Calculation: Coverage A & Coverage D
42:20 How to research 4-5 bedroom supply in your market
45:15 Ruben’s Insurance Napkin Math Example
- Purchase Price: $480k
- Atlanta Land Value- 10% on average
- Dwelling Value- $432k
- Loss of Use Value- $86k
48:40 Solve the problem in your market
51:05 B2B Contract Advice with relocation companies
54:10 B2B Contract Advice for arbitrage/partnership opportunities
55:00 Connect directly on Furnished Finder w/ no booking fees, no commissions, save thousands

Website Links:
https://www.furnishedfinder.com/ 
https://www.keycheck.com/ 
https://www.furnishedfinder.com/stats 

Ruben’s Listings on Furnished Finder:
https://www.furnishedfinder.com/members/profile?u=Ruben.Kanya 
Social: Ruben Kanya @therealestateexperiment

Enjoying our show? We would be honored to receive your 5* review:

https://open.spotify.com/show/4SvrXhCVRZMkbVDTF2Fyh2?si=f3d62047d84244a9

metadata.author: She's Got Assets™
metadata.shortDescription:
Shelter in the Storm | Partnering with Insurance for MTR Disaster Housing Solutions

This comprehensive series explores the intricacies of managing midterm rentals, especially in the context of disaster relief housing. Hosts Shona Lepis, She's Got Assets, Bonnie Low MTR Connect, Jon Wolf, mini stays delve into topics such as aligning housing supply with demand, transitioning from short-term to midterm rentals, and meeting the specific needs of disaster victims. The discussions highlight the critical role of insurance in furnishing accommodations and offer practical advice for property owners, including handling insurance placement, managing utilities, and optimizing listings on platforms like Furnished Finder and Airbnb. Key elements include the importance of tenant screening, flexibility in lease agreements, and pet-friendly accommodations. Additional segments introduce the Mini Stays platform—a new, efficient solution for midterm rentals—and provide a detailed walkthrough of its user-friendly features. Practical management tips, marketing strategies, and insights into leveraging temporary housing databases are also covered. The series concludes with Q&A sessions addressing common queries and sharing effective strategies for supporting community recovery.

metadata.title: Profitable Rentals with Purpose: Housing Displaced Families
metadata.author: FIRE ♦ Rich Rice
metadata.shortDescription:
00:19 Introduction – Why housing displaced families is a win-win strategy
02:05 Adrian’s Story – How he discovered this unique rental niche
04:12 The Model Explained – Step-by-step process from referral to move-in
06:25 Ideal Properties – What works best for insurance-paid rentals
08:10 Building Key Relationships – Connecting with adjusters and relocation companies
10:28 Scaling the Business – Adrian’s growth journey and lessons learned
12:42 Systems & Processes – How to keep operations smooth and stress-free
15:00 Benefits Beyond Profit – The human impact of helping families in crisis
17:20 Getting Started – Action steps for entering this niche
18:53 Wrap-Up – Final thoughts and encouragement to take the leap

In this insightful session, Adrian Espino reveals how he’s built a thriving rental business by providing housing for families displaced by disasters—paid for by insurance companies. 

You’ll learn how the process works, what properties fit best, how to form valuable industry relationships, and the systems needed to run it efficiently. 

This is more than a rental strategy—it’s a chance to make a real difference while generating dependable, often above-market income.

Subscribe to our channel now to transform your real estate investment approach and start making your investment dreams a reality TODAY! 🌟

Visit: https://www.firecenterhq.com for guides, classes, coaching and more!

metadata.title: Furnished Rentals in 2026: Forget Nurses & Insurance Claims
metadata.author: Midterm Rental Consulting
metadata.shortDescription:
Are midterm rentals still worth it in 2025 and beyond? This video breaks down the future of furnished 30+ day rentals, including how much money midterm rentals actually make, who your real tenant pool is (beyond traveling nurses), and how to stay consistently booked.

If you're a landlord or real estate investor trying to decide between short-term rentals, midterm rentals, or long-term rentals, this guide explains the differences in income, workload, and risk—so you can choose the best strategy for your goals.

You’ll learn:

📍 How much midterm rentals make vs long-term and Airbnb
📍 Why traveling nurses and insurance claims are NOT the best strategy
📍 The new tenant demand (work-from-anywhere, relocations, renovations, seasonal stays)
📍 The best property types for midterm rentals based on current demographic trends
📍 How to stay rented using platforms like Airbnb, Furnished Finder, Zillow, and Booking.com

Consulting
✅ Book consulting HERE: https://stan.store/erin_spradlin
✅ Get a free midterm rental lease here: https://stan.store/erin_spradlin

This video is based on real data from consulting with hundreds of landlords across the U.S. and years of firsthand experience managing furnished rentals.

If you're thinking about starting a midterm rental, switching from Airbnb, or optimizing your current rental strategy, this will help you make a smarter, more profitable decision.
_________________________________
WEBSITE
✅ Website: https://stan.store/erin_spradlin
💡 📚 My newsletter: https://erinspradlin.substack.com/
_________________________________

CHAPTERS

metadata.author: The CoLiving Insider
metadata.shortDescription:
Most master lease videos stop at the signature. That is where the real risk starts. In this video, we walk through five ways a master lease can blow up after you sign it, and the exact lease terms that protect you from each one.

In this video:
00:00 Introduction
0:47 Blow up 1: The owner sells the house
1:37 Blow up 2: The owner stops paying the mortgage (and what an S.N.D.A. is)
2:41 Blow up 3: The city shows up
3:41 Blow up 4: One resident stops paying
4:38 Blow up 5: The renewal squeeze
5:31 Bonus: The insurance claim that gets denied
6:50 What Quarters and Common teach about growing too fast
8:38 A master lease is only as strong as the paper it is written on

Watch next: 

How to Start Co-Living Without Buying a House (Master Lease Guide): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qqqkM3H9YY 

The Real Math on a "No Money Down" Co-Living House: https://youtu.be/XgG24Tjmt2k

Buy or Master Lease? https://youtu.be/i2EiHbkhJwg?si=9iQfi63AINClpVUw

Go deeper in this week's newsletter, including a house that fails the numbers and how one extra room fixes it: https://thecolivinginsider.com

Which of these five worries you most? Tell us in the comments.

This video is for education only and is not legal, tax, or financial advice. Lease, eviction, and foreclosure rules vary by state. Have a local real estate attorney review your lease before you sign.

The Co-Living Insider covers the co-living and shared housing model for real estate investors and operators.

#MasterLease #RentalArbitrage #colivingspace

Choosing the right furniture and essentials

Internet, utilities, and safety must-haves

Where to list for maximum bookings (and where not to waste time)

segments.text: You've heard the buzz about midterm
rentals. Maybe you've even run the
numbers and realized it actually makes
more sense than trying to fight for STR
bookings in an oversaturated market. But
now you're wondering, how the heck do I
set one of these up from scratch?
What do I need to furnish? What kind of
Wi-Fi do I need? Do I list it on Airbnb,
Zillow, furnish finders? All of the
above. and how do I make sure I attract
the right kind of guests? This video is
your full guide to setting up a midterm
rental from the ground up. Whether
you're turning your own property into an
MTR, converting a struggling Airbnb, or
furnishing a newly purchased rental,
this walkthrough will show you exactly
what to do, what to avoid, and how to
get it right the first time. So, let's
get into it. Midterm rentals or MTRs are
furnished rentals typically leased for
30 days or more. They attract travel
nurses, insurance displacements,
relocations, remote workers, and
families in transition. In Phoenix,
that's a growing pool of renters, and
the competition is still relatively low
compared to STRs. But here's the thing,
you can't just throw a bed and a couch
into a house and call it a day. There's
a difference between a furnish rental
and a functional midterm rental that
performs. I've helped investors across
Phoenix set up MTRS that not only
attract consistent 30 plus day guests,
but also run smoothly and require less
hands-on than you might think. But it
all starts with setup. Step one, define
your ideal guest. Before you buy
anything or create a listing, you need
to know who you're setting it up for.
Different guests expect different
things. If you're targeting travel
nurses, you need clean, cozy, and
efficient. These guests are often solo,
staying 13 weeks, and need a quiet place
to decompress. If you're targeting
insurance displacement guests like a
families whose home flooded or caught
fire, you'll need a setup that can
accommodate three to five people with a
fully stocked kitchen and a little more
homey com
and a little more homey comfort. If
you're looking to attract corporate
relocation or digital mo nomads, they'll
expect fast Wi-Fi, a good desk setup,
and more of a modern feel. Bottom line,
define your ideal guest first. That
decision informs everything else. Step
two, choose furniture and furnishings
strategically.
Here's the rule. Your place should feel
like a furnished apartment someone could
actually live in for a few months, not a
staged home for a magazine.
Start with the essentials. Beds in every
bedroom. Queen beds work best. Twins and
kid-friendly spaces. Quality mattresses.
Don't cheap out. People are living
there. Nightstands and lamps. Dressers
or closet storage with hangers. Sofa and
chairs in living room. Coffee table and
side tables. Dining table with four to
six chairs. Desk and a chair for working
professionals. Smart TV in the living
area. Area rugs if you have tile or
laminate flooring. curtains or blinds
for privacy.
Then layer in the functional extra full
kitchen setup, pots, pans, utensils,
plates, glasses, storage containers,
etc. Coffee maker, ideally a drip and a
curig or espresso. Microwave, toaster,
blender, cleaning supplies and broom and
mop. Laundry hamper and vacuum. Linens,
two full sets of sheets per bed. Towels,
two per guest minimum. Toiletry starter
kits, soap, shampoo, tepee, paper
towels, first aid kit, flashlight,
batteries. Make sure everything is
durable, neutral, and easy to clean.
Avoid fragile decor or anything
highmaintenance. Think stylish but
livable. Wayfair, Amazon, Target, and
IKEA are your go-to sourcing spots.
Bonus tip, don't go overboard on wall
art or decor. Too much Airbnb aesthetics
can backfire in the MTR world. You want
it to feel welcoming but not overly
themed. Step three, internet, utilities,
and safety features. Every MTR should
include utilities and internet as part
of the monthly rent. These guests aren't
setting up accounts or paying
separately. Make sure you have
high-speed internet, minimum 400 Mbps,
strong Wi-Fi signal in every room.
Consider a mesh network. Smart TV with
Netflix, Hulu, or streaming apps ready
to go. All utilities on and autopaid,
water, sewer, electric, trash, gas if
applicable. A digital lock, schlage, and
code is a favorite because it integrates
with platforms like owner and doesn't
need a hub. smoke detectors, fire
extinguishers, carbon monoxide
detectors, exterior security cameras
only facing entrance and disclosed in
your listing. It sounds like a lot, but
once it's set up, you're good. These
things create peace of mind for you and
the guest and reduce maintenance
headaches. Now, step four, decide your
pricing and your minimum stay. Midterm
rentals are priced monthly, not nightly.
But that doesn't mean you just guess at
this. Start with your comp research.
Furnish finder shows active monthly
rates by city and zip code. Airbnb with
a 30-day filter gives you nightly rates.
Just multiply that by 30 and adjust.
Facebook Marketplace and Travel Nurse
Groups offer some insight, too. In
Phoenix, monthly MTR rates range. Studio
and onebedrooms 22 to 2,800 a month. Two
bedrooms 2,800 to 4,000 a month,
depending on finishes and location.
Three beds, 3,800 to 5,500 a month for
high-end homes in desirable areas.
Set a 30-day minimum to avoid triggering
STR regulations and to target the right
guest. Most investors aim for 90%
occupancy with only three to six guest
turnovers per year. Step five, list your
property where MTR guests are actually
looking. This part is key and different
from STR.
You're going to need to list your MTR on
Furnish Finder, number one platform for
travel nurses and insurance housing.
Airbnb, yes, but only with a 30-day
minimum. Zillow plus apartments.com is
great for corporate and relocation
placements, Facebook groups, post in
local nurse housing and temporary rental
groups. Travel nursingousing travel
nurseousing.com another nurse specific
platform. When creating your listing,
focus on clean, professional photos.
Hire a photographer. Highlight what
makes your place liveable. long-term
desk setup, laundry, full kitchen.
Include a list of what's provided. Be
clear about policies. No pets, no
smoking, etc. Add local convenience
details. 8 minutes to Mayo Clinic, 5
minutes to Banner Desert, fast Wi-Fi,
and fully stock kitchen included. Most
of your MTR guests won't care about a
hot tub or putting green. They want
reliable cleanliness and ease of moving.
Now, step six, guest screening and lease
agreements. Unlike STRs, MTRS often
involve signing a lease or agreement,
even if it's booked through Airbnb or
Furnish Finders. Here's how I handle it.
Every guest must submit an ID and sign a
lease agreement. I collect a refundable
security deposit. We run a soft
background check if booked direct. I use
tools like tenant cloud or owner to send
agreements and collect payment. Make
sure your agreement outlines dates of
stay, rent and deposit terms, guest
responsibilities,
rules about guests, pets, noise, etc.
Maintenance procedure, what's included
and what isn't. This protects both you
and the guests. And yes, I help my
clients set all of this up so they don't
have to figure it out alone.
Step seven, automation and management
systems. While MTRs are lower touch than
STRs, they still require systems. You'll
want to automate rent collection and
lease signing, coordinate cleaning
between guests, handle maintenance
requests quickly, track expenses for tax
time, keep communication professional
and timely. I personally use tools like
owner for messaging, calendar and lease
automation, Google Sheets or QuickBooks
for finances, turnover B&B or simple
cleaner text thread for scheduling,
Google voice or WhatsApp for guest
communication.
If that all sounds like a lot, I get it.
That's exactly why many investors have
me manage this for them. It's still a
business even if it's not a nightly
guest churn like Airbnb. Step eight,
reinvest in your guest experience. Even
though your guests are staying longer,
reviews still matter and many MTR guests
are repeat travelers, especially travel
nurses. Do the little things that create
big return. A clean, welcoming home.
Fast, friendly communication.
Clear check-in instructions. A small
welcome basket with snacks or coffee.
Mid-stage check-in. Just saying, "Hey,
just checking in to make sure
everything's going smoothly. Let me know
if you need anything." Good guests
attract more good guests. And building a
strong reputation is how your property
stays full year round. Step nine, you
need to track performance and scale.
What works? After your first MTR guest,

metadata.title: Your Lease Expired — You Don't Have to Leave (and Other Void Lease Clauses)
metadata.author: Ontario Renter Rights
metadata.shortDescription:
Your one-year lease ends and the message arrives: sign a new lease or move out. In Ontario, expiry is not a termination ground. This episode covers: (1) s. 38(1) — when a fixed term ends unrenewed and unterminated, landlord and tenant are DEEMED to have renewed it as a MONTHLY tenancy on the SAME terms (rent rises only under Part VII); no signature required; (2) s. 4(1) — a tenancy-agreement provision INCONSISTENT with the Act is VOID, and s. 3(1) — the Act applies despite any agreement or waiver; (3) s. 14 — a 'no pets' provision is VOID (the lease clause itself; condo rules and municipal bylaws are separate regimes); (4) s. 15 — ACCELERATION clauses (all remaining rent due on a default) are VOID. Plus the reading method: find the section the clause collides with — ss. 105/106 deposits, s. 20 repairs, ss. 25–27 entry, s. 108 post-dated cheques.

General information about Ontario rental law — not legal advice.

Free help:
• Landlord and Tenant Board: 1-888-332-3234 · tribunalsontario.ca
• Community legal clinics (via Legal Aid Ontario): 1-800-668-8258
• Advocacy Centre for Tenants Ontario: acto.ca

Ontario Renter Rights — plain-language Ontario rental-law education for renters in apartments, rooming / multi-tenant houses, basement units, rented condos, student housing and personal-care homes.

a new lease, accept new terms, or move out. It sounds
like a deadline with your home attached to it. In Ontario,
the law answered this question in advance, and the answer is
that nothing ends. Today, what really happens when a lease expires,
and which clauses in a lease were never worth the paper?
General information about Ontario rental law, not legal advice. Stay to
the end for where to get free help with your own
case. The renewal that happens by itself, section 38. Section 38,
subsection 1 of the Residential Tenancies Act. If a fixed -term
tenancy ends and has not been renewed or terminated, the landlord
and the tenant are deemed to have renewed it as a
monthly tenancy, on the same terms as the expired tenancy, subject
only to rent increases made in accordance with the act. Deemed
means the law does it for you. No new signature is
required. No new lease has to be negotiated. The tenancy simply
continues, month to month, with the same terms it had the
day before it expired. Subsections 2 and 3 do the same
for daily, weekly, monthly, and other periodic tendencies. So the honest
answer to, my lease expired, do I have to leave, is
no. Expiry is not a termination ground, and it never has
been under this act. What month to month actually changes? Two
things change, and everything else stays. First, the rhythm. Instead of
a fixed term, the tenancy now runs period to period, month
to month for most renters. Second, flexibility. If you later decide
to leave, tenant notice rules apply to the periodic tenancy rather
than a fixed end date. What does not change? Your rent
can still only rise under the rent increase rules from episode
14. The notice, the 90 days, the 12 month rule, the
guideline. Your landlord's duties do not change. Your rights do not
shrink. And a landlord who wants the unit back still needs
a lawful ground, the proper form, and the board process from
episode 16. A landlord may offer a new fixed term, some
tenants like the certainty, but an offer is a choice, not
an obligation. The master rule for bad clauses, section 4. In
the new clauses, section 4, subsection 1. A provision in a
tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with the act or the regulations
is void. Void means it never had legal effect, not that
it is unfair, not that a judge might dislike it, but
that it does not count, even though you signed it, even
though it is printed in bold. Section 3, subsection 1, is
the reason why. The act applies despite any agreement or waiver
to the contrary. You cannot sign away the act's protections, and
a landlord cannot draft around them. So when Elise says something

metadata.title: When to Switch from Airbnb to Mid-Term Rentals (Phoenix Investors Need to Hear This)
metadata.author: The Furnished Rental Strategist
metadata.shortDescription:
Wondering when to pivot from Airbnb to mid-term rentals? In this video, we break down exactly how to decide between short-term rentals (STR) and mid-term rentals (MTR), especially in the Phoenix market. If your Airbnb isn’t cash flowing, dealing with high vacancy, or burning you out, this will help you understand what’s actually working right now and how to pivot strategically.

We cover real investor scenarios, market trends, and how to evaluate whether switching to mid-term rentals makes sense for your property and goals.

If you're investing in Phoenix real estate, Airbnb, or furnished rentals, this is a must-watch.

If you're serious about buying or optimizing a short-term or mid-term rental, I’ve put together a quick intake form to understand your goals before setting up a strategy call: https://staciemuller46977.activehosted.com/f/4

Website: www.housetohomecollective.com
Instagram: @stacie_sells_az

⬆️⬆️⬆️ Ready to transform your investment into a high-performing MTR? Let’s make it happen. ⬆️⬆️⬆️

☀️ TO GET IN TOUCH WITH ME
Stacie Muller
REALTOR® | MTR Investment & Management Specialist
West USA Realty | Chandler AZ
Email: realtorstacie@staciemuller.com

INSTAGRAM ⇢ @stacie_sells_az
WEBSITE ⇢ www.housetohomecollective.com
FACEBOOK ⇢ facebook.com/StacieSmallMuller

With over 20 years in real estate, I help investors create hands-free, income-producing homes through mid-term rental strategy, property setup, and full-service management.

If you’re sitting on an underperforming Airbnb or traditional rental, I’ll show you how to reposition it for reliable MTR income—and build long-term equity at the same time.

Subscribe if you’re ready to learn how smart investors are building wealth through Arizona mid-term rentals.

And now for the boring but legally required licensing information: 
West USA Realty 
1850 E Northrop Blvd #170 
Chandler, AZ 85286 

Please note: commissions are always negotiable and always have been, no matter what the news headlines say. If you have questions about the recent NAR lawsuit and what this means whether you're selling or buying, I'd love to explain how it will affect you.

The Benefits of Roofers and Public Adjusters Working Together - David Dube - Claims Game Podcast 034

Roofers vs public adjusters OR roofers WITH public adjusters?

There are many benefits that come to the joint work of roofers and public adjusters and make it very difficult for the insurance company to fight you on anything.

Both sides have their own book of business, referral sources, and ways of getting business and because of that the two of them combined are just dynamite!

Our guest today is David Dube, the owner, and CEO of The Lawgical Firm P.A.

David Dube is licensed by the State of Florida to adjust and litigate all insurance claims. For many years, he worked as an adjuster and appraiser all throughout the state of Florida.

 - The Advantages of Roofing Contractors and PAs working together
 - Assignment of Benefits Law

metadata.shortDescription:
#Airbnb2026 #Airbnbpodcast2026 #howtoairbnb2026 
Discover how Humza Zafar scaled from a 9–5 engineer to over 300 Airbnb units across the United States and why most operators fail once they try to scale beyond 5 units.

In this episode, Humza explains:

✅ how he scaled from 0 to 100 units in under two years
✅ why most operators cannibalize their own profits when scaling
✅ the real difference between 5 units and 100 units
✅ why luxury units outperform studios in 2026
✅ how operational complexity kills margins at scale
✅ the importance of cash reserves and avoiding debt traps
✅ why bad reviews are the fastest way to ruin your Airbnb business
✅ how he built a remote team that allows him to work only 3 hours per week
✅ why “location doesn’t matter” is the worst advice online

Humza shares the raw reality of scaling a serious Airbnb operation from million-dollar months to costly mistakes, operational pressure, and the mindset required to build real freedom.

If you’re serious about launching or scaling your Airbnb portfolio, Humza runs a private Operator Community where he breaks down:

* Real deal analysis (live)
* Market validation frameworks
* Landlord pitch systems
* Pricing & automation strategies
* Scaling from 1 → 5+ units

This is not a passive course.
It’s an execution room for serious operators.

$99/month — full system access.
14-day trial available.

👉 Join here: https://www.skool.com/airbnbaccelerator/about

If you’re building, I’ll see you inside.

metadata.author: Rich Somers
metadata.shortDescription:
On today’s episode, Rich sits down with Ruben Kanya – Mid-Term Rental Specialist & Investor, Co-Founder of Invested Escapes, Podcast Host of The Real Estate Experiment,  and Author of Hospitable Hosts. Ruben helps real estate investors 3x their returns without changing or disrupting their existing short-term rental operation by adding the mid-term rental insurance strategy. Ruben owns half a dozen properties between Atlanta and Cape Cod, Massachusetts, and also controls more than 30 properties within his nationwide network — where he and his team have brokered and/or co-hosted mid-term rental insurance contracts for other investors.

Rich and Ruben start off by discussing Ruben’s takeaways from Jesse Vasquez’s mid-term rental conference, the benefits of real estate and mid-term rentals, the real estate market in Georgia, leveraging real estate, Codie Sanchez, the negotiation of equity, and the baby boomer business opportunities.

They then reflect on defining mid term rentals, Ruben’s negotiations with insurance companies, relocation and staffing agencies, hybrid modeling mid-term rentals, the issues that Ruben is solving in this community, the average premiums of mid-term rentals. insurance companies and public adjusters, what mid-term rentals rent for, and adding fees to reoccurring revenue.

Lastly, they talk about arbitraging, the biggest risks to mid-term rentals, corporate housing, depreciating cashflow, how to get started in mid-term rentals, the best places to list, how to list mid-term rentals on Airbnb, Ruben’s mastermind, Mike Sjogren, Ruben’s trip to the west coast, Ruben’s inspiration, and the benefits of podcasting. 
 
Connect with Ruben on Instagram: @therealestateexperiment

Connect with Rich on Instagram: @rich_somers

Interested in investing with Somers Capital? Visit www.somerscapital.com/invest to learn more.

Interested in joining our Boutique Hotel Mastermind? Visit www.somerscapital.com/mastermind to book a free call.

Interested in STR/Boutique Hotel Management? Visit www.excelsiorstays.com/management to book a free call.

metadata.title: Landlords: Always (Always, Always) Require Renters Insurance—Here’s Why | Daily Podcast
metadata.author: BiggerPockets
metadata.shortDescription:
Sure, renters insurance is vital to cover a tenant's personal belongings. However, it's imperative that landlords require renters insurance on any new lease or lease renewal. Why? Renters insurance doesn't just protect tenants; it's useful for landlords if they need to cover a tenant's losses caused by someone else.

So, renters insurance has numerous benefits for both landlords and tenants.

Despite this fact, renters insurance might sound like an extra expense that tenants think they can do without. In fact, if a landlord doesn't require it, it's unlikely that most renters will take out insurance. They may even believe that the landlord's insurance covers all their personal belongings. But similar to most insurance policies, it's only "an unnecessary expense" until the worst happens, and you need to file a claim.

This article examines the many reasons why it’s a good idea to require that your tenants take out renters insurance.

What Does Renters Insurance Cover?
As with any insurance, coverage depends on the policy taken out and the terms and conditions. Generally, renters insurance covers the following:

Damages to personal property
Liability for injuries
Losses caused by theft
Natural disasters
Relocation expenses if the rental unit is uninhabitable

https://www.biggerpockets.com/blog/why-landlords-must-require-renters-insurance

metadata.title: Airbnb's New Rules: Are Hosts at Risk? | Myka Artis
metadata.author: Vivian Yip
metadata.shortDescription:
Airbnb's changing policies are raising serious questions for short-term and mid-term rental hosts. Are property owners losing control over guest screening, rental agreements, and the ability to protect their investments?

In this episode, Vivian sits down with Myka Artis, an experienced Airbnb and mid-term rental operator since 2017, to discuss how the short-term rental industry has evolved and what these changes mean for property owners.

From Airbnb's November 20 policy changes to guest verification, security deposits, and rental agreements, they explore why hosts need to rethink their strategies and take a more proactive approach to protecting their properties.

Myka shares his experience managing rental properties across Texas and Arkansas, why he believes larger homes are often better suited for mid-term rentals, and how building the right systems can make managing properties remotely more efficient.

They also discuss the importance of diversifying booking channels, building direct bookings, working with local governments, and partnering with insurance providers to establish stronger protections for rental operators.

IN THIS EPISODE, YOU'LL DISCOVER:

• How Airbnb has evolved since 2017 and what the latest policy changes mean for hosts.
• Why guest IDs, rental agreements, and security deposits matter when protecting rental properties.
• Why Micah believes three- to five-bedroom homes offer more opportunities for mid-term rental investors.
• How to evaluate properties for insurance stays, traveling professionals, families, and construction crews.
• Why short-term and mid-term rental strategies can work together.
• How to build systems for managing rental properties remotely.
• How AI can simplify property management workflows and automate business processes.
• Why hosts should diversify beyond Airbnb through direct bookings and Vrbo.
• How working with local governments and insurance companies can help protect rental properties.
• What hosts should know about Furnished Finder's potential property management system integrations.
• How the Step-Up MTR system helped Micah secure a valuable booking opportunity.

If you want more detail, The Airbnb Blueprint is my Skool community. It's $59 a month and the first 7 days are free:
https://www.skool.com/the-airbnb-blueprint-rafaloza/about

22:55 Choosing your market and your customer

metadata.title: R-3 | Airbnb Taxes 2026: Landlord, Business or Hotel? (14-Day Rule, 7-Day Rule, Schedule E or C)
metadata.author: Restart Tax Talk
metadata.shortDescription:
R-3, the third video in the Rental Property Owners series. You listed your place on Airbnb or Vrbo — to the IRS that makes you a landlord, a business, or a hotel, and the answer decides whether you pay self-employment tax, whether your losses count against your salary, and whether some of the income is tax-free. In five minutes: the 14-day rule (rent your home 14 days or fewer and the rent is tax-free), the 7-day rule that takes a short-term rental out of the passive loss rules, what "hotel-style services" means and when Schedule C and 15.3% self-employment tax apply, the material participation hours test (500 hours, or 100 hours and more than anyone else), a worked cost segregation example on a $600,000 beach house, the three catches, the personal-use test (14 days or 10% of rented days), what counts as income and the $20,000 / 200-transaction 1099-K threshold, the city hotel tax and license, and the four mistakes that get hosts IRS letters.

Chapters
0:00 Landlord, business or hotel?
0:26 The 14-day rule: tax-free rent
0:43 The 7-day rule: which schedule are you on?
1:09 Hotel-style services vs normal hosting (Schedule C vs E)
1:30 The door: material participation — 500 hours, or 100 and more than anyone else
1:58 The numbers: a $600,000 beach house, cost segregation and 100% bonus
2:25 Three catches: real hours, recapture, California
2:46 Personal use: the 14-day / 10% test
3:09 What counts as income, and the 1099-K
3:33 Then your city: the hotel tax, the certificate and the license
3:53 Four things that get letters
4:13 What a former IRS Revenue Agent asks for: the calendar decides
4:34 Wrap-up

2026 figures and rules: a dwelling unit used as a residence and rented for fewer than 15 days in the year — the rent is excluded from income and no rental expenses are deducted (IRC §280A(g)); an activity is not a "rental activity" for the passive loss rules when the average period of customer use is 7 days or less, or 30 days or less with significant personal services (Temp. Reg. §1.469-1T(e)(3)(ii)); material participation tests — more than 500 hours, or more than 100 hours and not less than any other individual, or substantially all of the participation (Temp. Reg. §1.469-5T(a)); rental income is excluded from self-employment tax unless substantial services are provided for the occupant's convenience beyond those needed to maintain the space (IRC §1402(a)(1); Reg. §1.1402(a)-4(c); Chief Counsel Advice 202151005); self-employment tax 15.3%; personal use of more than the greater of 14 days or 10% of the days rented at fair rental makes the unit a residence, so expenses are allocated and rental deductions are limited to rental income (IRC §280A(d), (e), (c)(5)); days spent substantially full time on repairs and maintenance are not personal-use days; 100% bonus depreciation for qualified property acquired and placed in service after January 19, 2025 (IRC §168(k) as amended by P.L. 119-21), California does not conform; Form 1099-K is required from third-party settlement organizations only above $20,000 and 200 transactions (IRC §6050W as amended by P.L. 119-21); excess business losses above $256,000 ($512,000 joint) are carried forward (IRC §461(l); Rev. Proc. 2025-32); City of San Diego transient occupancy tax 11.75% to 13.75% by zone, TOT certificate required for any stay under one month, short-term residential occupancy license fees $193 to $1,129 for two years. Example in the video: $600,000 purchase, $450,000 building, 25% reclassified to 5- and 15-year property by a cost segregation study = $112,500 deducted in year one; roughly $40,000 of federal tax saved in the 32% bracket.

The 5-Minute CPA: one tax question, answered in five minutes, from Restart Financial Services, a San Diego CPA firm led by a licensed CPA and former IRS Revenue Agent. Serving clients in all 50 states. Fixed fees, quoted in writing. Narrated by an AI voice; written and reviewed by the CPA. Music: "Angel's Dream" by Aakash Gandhi (YouTube Audio Library).

metadata.title: A Legal Guide for Airbnb Hosts: New Jersey's Short-Term Rental Laws by Christine Matus
metadata.author: The Matus Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
A Legal Guide for Airbnb Hosts: New Jersey's Short-Term Rental Laws by Christine Matus 

New Jersey real estate attorney Christine Matus breaks down short-term rental laws in Monmouth County for Airbnb hosts before they buy or list a property.

New Jersey treats short-term rentals as a formal business activity, meaning hosts face real tax obligations, municipal permit requirements, and zoning enforcement. The state's regulatory framework operates on two independent layers. At the state level, New Jersey classifies most short-term stays as transient accommodations subject to Sales Tax and the State Occupancy Fee. Stays of 30 days or fewer fall under transient lodging rules, while longer stays may trigger landlord-tenant protections. Bookings made through platforms like Airbnb or Vrbo generally activate state tax obligations automatically, while direct bookings from hosts with fewer than three New Jersey units may qualify for an exemption — though local zoning rules still apply regardless.

Being registered with the New Jersey Division of Taxation does not shield a host from local enforcement. In Monmouth County, there is no single county-wide ordinance, so rules shift dramatically between municipalities. Asbury Park limits short-term rentals to owner-occupied primary residences, making non-owner-occupied listings a code violation. Howell Township imposes fines starting at one thousand dollars for unregistered rentals, with escalating penalties for continued violations. Red Bank's enforcement actions can reach the property owner, the rental agent, or any responsible party. High-traffic areas near the Asbury Park Boardwalk, Monmouth Park Racetrack, and Pier Village in Long Branch draw heightened scrutiny. Violations can result in daily fines, cease-and-desist orders, or appearances before municipal court.

HOA and condo board bylaws add a risk layer that title searches alone do not catch. A real estate attorney reviewing those documents before closing can identify hidden rental bans and occupancy restrictions that would make a short-term rental strategy unworkable. The Matus Law Group conducts due diligence on municipal restrictions, reviews HOA bylaws, and structures business entities to protect personal assets.

metadata.title: I Built My Corporate Housing Business BACKWARDS (And It Works Better)
metadata.author: Jorge Garcia | Roadmap Lodging
metadata.shortDescription:
Corporate housing inquiries: 1-855-552-9155 Most people build their corporate housing business the wrong way.
They sign a lease… furnish a unit… upload it online… and then sit there hoping a booking magically shows up.

That’s backwards.

In this video, I’m breaking down how I built my corporate housing business “backwards”, starting with demand first, not the property, and why it works dramatically better.

If you’re tired of relying on Airbnb, unpredictable occupancy, or guessing your way through this industry… this is the mindset shift that changes everything.

My 3-Step Backwards Method

1️⃣ Find the demand
Call relocation managers, insurance adjusters, travel nurse coordinators, HR directors, and learn what they need.

2️⃣ Build the relationship
Become the go-to solution, not just another Airbnb listing.

3️⃣ THEN find the property
Match the unit to the needs, not the other way around.

This is how you eliminate 90% of the risks that kill most operators.

What This Approach Creates:

✔ Pre-committed bookings
✔ Long-term corporate stays
✔ Predictable monthly income
✔ Freedom from Airbnb algorithms
✔ A business that runs on systems, not luck

You don’t need 15 units.
You just need 5 strong relationships.

metadata.title: Land 90 Day Corporate Housing Contracts
metadata.author: Jorge Garcia | Roadmap Lodging
metadata.shortDescription:
Corporate housing inquiries: 1-855-552-9155 If you feel like you’re playing Airbnb roulette, sweating over algorithm updates, praying the next booking isn’t a one-night party, and watching profits get eaten by turnovers, this episode is your exit ramp. In this deep dive, we break down Jorge Garcia’s Roadmap Lodging playbook for pivoting from B2C short-term rentals to B2B corporate housing (think relocations, insurance displacement, project teams, and traveling nurses), where 60–90 day stays are normal and stability beats “vibes.” You’ll learn why most hosts fail (they try to “Airbnb” their way into corporate), what a real B2B-ready unit actually needs (bulletproof Wi-Fi, blackout curtains, a real desk + ergonomic chair, full kitchen setup, washer/dryer, extra linens), and why “cute design” loses to “functional living” every time. We also cover the credibility stack that gets you treated like a vendor, one-pager PDF, simple website, domain email (no Gmail), and a Google Business Profile so you own reviews outside the platforms. Finally, we walk through the practical outreach system that wins deals without being spammy: a tight hit list (HR, adjusters, recruiters, realtors) and the 5-emails-per-week habit that compounds into a real pipeline, so you’re no longer waiting on an app to decide your income.

metadata.title: 5 Things You Need to Know About Breaking Your Lease
metadata.author: The Legal Aid Society
metadata.shortDescription:
Breaking your lease early can be complicated. Debt can follow a person even after they have left their apartment, and you may be liable for the months of rent that are left on your lease should you leave the apartment before your lease expires - potentially impacting your credit or ability to find new housing.

Watch Legal Aid's video "5 Things You Need to Know About Breaking Your Lease" to learn how to approach your landlord about breaking your lease, and the steps you can take to avoid negative financial consequences.

00:45 2. Steps to Break Your Lease
01:24 3. Duty to Mitigate
01:42 4. Breaking a Lease without Penalty
02:30 5. Consequences of Breaking Your Lease

metadata.title: What to do if my Tenant Breaks the Lease Agreement?
metadata.author: The Listing Real Estate Management
metadata.shortDescription:
Owning a rental property can come with its fair share of complications or difficult situations, especially if you’re not experienced and self-managing your rental property.

As a professional property management company, we know all too well one common issue self-managing landlords deal with is their tenant breaking the lease agreement.

So, if you are a landlord or rental property owner and have not dealt with this situation, chances are you’ll encounter it in due time. If your tenant breaks the lease, it may affect your property and financial situation and cause a lot of time to find a new one.

Check out the Full Blog Post below 🏡⬇️

https://thelistingrem.com/what-to-do-if-my-tenant-breaks-the-lease-agreement/

What happens if your tenant vacates early and broke their lease agreement?

First, you’ll want to look at your lease agreement and determine if you already have a lease default or early termination clause written in your lease agreement. If you do, you will need to follow the terms of your lease agreement.

If you don’t have this written into your lease agreement, you’ll want to add this as soon as possible. Having a roadmap already in place will help with knowing what to do if this happens and help the tenant understand that they are signing a contract they are responsible for rather than a short-term obligation.

Once you’ve determined your lease default penalty, you’ll want to ensure that the terms are followed. For example, if you require two months to break the lease agreement, you’ll want to receive this before your tenant vacates the premises.

What happens if my tenant vacates without notice?

If you have an irresponsible tenant that provides no prior notice, they will be breaking their lease; it may be more challenging to collect the lease break fee.

Regardless, if you cannot get a hold of your tenant, you’ll want to make sure you complete your security deposit disposition which is a notice you need to provide to claim their security deposit.

You’ll want to include your lease break fee on the security deposit claim form. Each state has different security deposit requirements, so you’ll want to understand this first.

Once your tenant receives your security deposit claim form with the due amount, they will either pay or not. One benefit of using a professional property management company is they will typically send the tenant to collections to receive the outstanding balance due.

What are common lease break fees?

1. Typically, the most common lease break fee is two months lease break fee and a forfeited security deposit.

2. Another standard lease break fee or term in a lease agreement is that your tenant is responsible for ongoing rental payments until you find another tenant to replace your current one.

How to reduce your tenant from breaking the lease agreement?

1. Tenant Screening - Single handily, the most crucial aspect of owning and managing a successful rental property is to screen your prospective tenants properly.

2. Lease Default or Early Termination - A solid lease agreement for your rental property will help reduce rental property risks. If you don’t have this section in your lease agreement, you can permanently attach an addendum to your lease stating your early termination requirements.

3. Leasing Red Flags - If you are showing your rental home to prospective renters, there are specific red flags that can help determine if they will be reliable tenants.

So what to do if your tenant does break the lease?

You’ll need to follow the terms of your lease agreement; otherwise, if you don’t have a lease default section in your lease, you’ll want to research what your state requirements are.

For example, here in the state of Florida -  Florida Statutes 83.595 states a landlord can charge up to 2 months of rent for lease default or liquidated damages.

Make sure you check your state requirements to see what you can charge your tenant for breaking their lease agreement.

If you have any questions or want to learn more about our Property Management Services, Contact us today! 🏡

https://thelistingrem.com/contact-us/

metadata.title: Want Out of Your Lease Early? The Real Cost of Breaking It
metadata.author: 60SecondLaw
metadata.shortDescription:
Need to move but your lease isn't up? Breaking a lease doesn't have to ruin you financially — but doing it wrong will. This video breaks down what leases actually require, your state's early-termination rules, the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (military), and the 3 steps to get out with minimal damage. Plus 5 mistakes that cost tenants thousands.

CHAPTERS
00:00 Dream job, 8 months left on your lease?
00:52 Not a lawyer — read this first
01:27 The duty to mitigate — they must re-rent
02:40 Early termination fees + buyouts
03:33 SCRA — the military exit ramp
04:29 Step 1 — read the lease, give notice
05:24 Step 2 — negotiate the buyout
06:11 Step 3 — mitigate + sublet or assignment
07:09 5 mistakes that cost money
08:12 Know your rights

📚 SOURCES
- Cornell Legal Information Institute: 50 U.S.C. §§ 3901-4043 (Servicemembers Civil Relief Act)
  https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/50/3901
- Your state's landlord-tenant statutes (early termination rules vary by state)
- Nolo: Breaking a lease guides
  https://www.nolo.com/

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
This video is for general legal information only — it is NOT legal advice, and I am not your lawyer. Landlord-tenant law is extremely state-specific. Use this video to understand the framework, then check your state's current rules and your lease. Consult a licensed attorney in your state before acting.

#BreakingLease #TenantRights #KnowYourRights #60SecondLaw

metadata.title: How To Break A Lease Early (And Avoid Getting Taken to Court)

metadata.shortDescription:
Official Lease Termination Letter: http://go.eforms.com/termination-letter-early

A lease is an agreement between someone who owns something and someone who wants to use it for a period of time. When you sign a lease for a property, you’re agreeing to make payments to your landlord for a time, and your landlord is agreeing to let you live in that place for that time. 

But we’re human, and we can’t control whether we get sick and need to move into a care facility during that year, whether we lose a job, or what unexpected circumstances we’ll run into. Whether you’re a tenant or a landlord, breaking a lease can expose you to financial and legal risks. But it’s possible, and there are ways to minimize your risk. Watch for things to think about if you’re considering breaking your lease so you can avoid being taken to court.


DISCLAIMER: This video is strictly for educational purposes and is in no way intended to provide legal advice. We do not make any warranties about the completeness, reliability, and accuracy of this information. Any action you take upon the information on this video is strictly at your own risk, and we will not be liable for any losses and damages in connection with the use of our videos.

metadata.shortDescription:
Domestic violence and breaking your lease early: how survivor early termination laws work, with Washington, Oregon and Illinois rules and HUD VAWA protections (US). https://www.readingdlaw.com
Educational only — not legal advice. Laws vary by state/city and lease.
Watch the full library: https://www.readingdlaw.com/videos

If you are in danger, call 911. National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788 (https://www.thehotline.org).

This is not a substitute for local legal aid, a victim advocate or a licensed attorney. No attorney-client relationship.

Chapters:
0:00 Domestic violence and breaking a lease: US overview and safety
0:37 Need to leave, but the lease has months left
1:08 How survivor early termination laws work
1:51 Washington: 90-day window and end-of-month rent
2:45 Oregon: 14 days written notice and release
3:36 Illinois Safe Homes Act: notice within 3 days
4:15 HUD housing: VAWA protections and emergency transfers
5:03 Seven-step plan to leave a lease safely
5:52 Myths and mistakes about breaking a lease after abuse
6:39 Recap: safety first, written notice and proof

Sources (official text):
Washington RCW 59.18.575 (written notice; protection order or qualified third-party report; 90 days; rent through end of month; full deposit): https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=59.18.575
Oregon ORS 90.453 (at least 14 days written notice with verification; 90 days; no rent or damages after release date; no termination fee): https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors090.html
Illinois Safe Homes Act, 765 ILCS 750/15 and 750/30 (written notice before or within 3 days of vacating; no waiver in lease): https://ilga.gov/legislation/ilcs/ilcs3.asp?ActID=2817&ChapterID=62
HUD VAWA rules, 24 CFR 5.2005 (no eviction for being a victim; emergency transfer plans) and 5.2003 (covered programs): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-24/section-5.2005
Official sources reviewed Nov 20, 2026 ET. Other states have different laws, and some have none. Notice, proof and rent rules depend on your state, lease and housing program.

segments.text: Disclaimer, whether you can end a lease
early because of domestic violence
depends on your state, your lease, and
your housing program.
This is general educational information
for United States renters, not legal
advice.
Rules vary by state, city, and lease.
This video does not create an
attorney-client relationship or replace
advice from a licensed attorney or local
legal aid.
If you are in danger right now, call
The National Domestic Violence Hotline
or text the word start to 88788.
You need to get out of your apartment to
be safe, but the lease still has 9
months left and you are afraid of owing
all of that rent.
That fear keeps a lot of people stuck.
Here is the good news.
A number of states have special early
exit laws for survivors of domestic
violence, sexual assault, and stalking.
Today we cover what these laws usually
require. Real rules from Washington,
Oregon, and Illinois, what changes in
HUD assisted housing, and a calm
seven-step plan.
Start with the pattern.
These laws are often called survivor or
victim early termination laws.
They usually let a tenant end a lease
without paying rent for the rest of the
term,
but they come with conditions.
Most require written notice to the
landlord.
Many require some kind of proof, like a
protection order, a police report, or a
signed statement from an advocate or
other qualified person.
Many have a time window after the abuse,
and you may still owe rent up to a set
date.
Not every state has a law like this, and
the details are different everywhere.
Free guides in every episode are at
readingd law.com.
Washington is a detailed example.
Under RCW 59.18.575,
a tenant who notifies the landlord in
writing that are a household member was
a victim of domestic violence, sexual
assault, unlawful harassment, or
stalking may end the rental agreement if
they have a valid protection order or a
signed written record of a report to a
qualified third party, such as a law
enforcement officer, a licensed health
professional, or a domestic violence
advocate.
The request must happen within 90 days
of the incident.
The tenant is released from rent after
the last day of the month they move out,
so the rent for that month is usually
still owed.
Washington also says the tenant is
entitled to the full deposit back, even
if the lease has an early termination
forfeiture clause, subject to the normal
rules for damage.
Other tenants on the lease are generally
not released.
Oregon uses a notice period.
Under ORS 90.453,
if a tenant gives the landlord at least
14 days written notice asking to be
released, the landlord must release the
tenant and any listed immediate family
members.
The notice must give the release date
and come with verification, such as a
valid protective order, a police report,
a conviction, or a signed statement from
a qualified third party like an
advocate, attorney, or health
professional.
The abuse must have happened within the
90 days before the notice, unless the
tenant is protected by a valid order.
After the release date, the tenant is
not liable for rent or damages incurred
after that date and cannot be charged a
fee just for ending the lease.
Other tenants stay on the lease.
The landlord also generally may not
share the information you provide.
Illinois works a little differently.
Under the Safe Homes Act, 765 ILCS 750,
Section 15, if a landlord sues for rent
after a tenant moves out, the tenant has
a defense and is not liable for rent
after they vacate if they were under a
credible, imminent threat of domestic or
sexual violence at the home and they
gave the landlord written notice of that
reason before moving out or within three
days after.
There is a separate path when sexual
violence happened on the premises with a
60-day window and supporting documents.
The act says these rights cannot be
waived in a lease.
Rent owed before you leave is still
owed.
If you live in HUD-assisted housing,
federal violence against women act rules
add protections
under 24 CFR 5.2005
in covered programs, including public
housing and section eight rental
assistance, a tenant cannot be denied
assistance or evicted because they are
or have been a victim of domestic
violence, dating violence, sexual
assault, or stalking if they otherwise
qualify.
Covered housing providers must also have
an emergency transfer plan.
A tenant can qualify for an emergency
transfer if they ask for it and
reasonably believe they face a threat of
imminent harm from further violence by
staying in the unit or for sexual
assault if it happened on the premises
within the last 90 days.
Ask your housing authority or property
manager for their plan in writing.
Here is a seven-step plan.
One, make a safety plan first.
An advocate at the hotline can help, and
your safety matters more than the
paperwork.
Two, find out whether your state has a
survivor early termination law and read
your lease.
Three, gather the kind of proof your
state accepts, like a protection order,
a police report, or a signed advocate
statement.
Four, give the landlord written notice
the way your law requires with the dates
it asks for.
Five, keep copies of everything and
write down when and how you delivered
it.
Six, when you leave, return the keys and
give a safe forwarding address for your
deposit.
Seven, talk to legal aid or a victim
advocate before you sign any lease break
agreement or pay a fee.
Three myths to leave behind.
Myth one, if you flee abuse, you
automatically owe every month left on
the lease.
Reality, some states release survivors
from future rent when they follow the
steps.
Myth two, the landlord can share why you
left with anyone.
Reality, states like Oregon limit what a
landlord may disclose.
Myth three, these laws work the same
everywhere.
Reality, notice periods, proof, and rent
rules are different in every state, and
some states have no special law at all.
Three mistakes to avoid.
Do not leave without giving written
notice if your law requires it.
Do not miss the deadline.
And do not assume a co-tenant who caused
harm gets the same release you do.
Recap, safety comes first, then check
your state law. Give written notice the
way it requires, include the proof it
asks for, and keep copies.
Educational only, not legal advice.
Talk to local legal aid, a victim
advocate, or a licensed attorney about
your situation, and please do not share
personal details in the comments.
Subscribe for more plain English renter
explainers and tell us your state in the
comments.
Optional support is on Cash App at
dollar sign reading d law.
Free guides in every episode are at
reading d law dot com.

metadata.title: Should You Rent Out Your House or Sell It?
metadata.author: House Math
metadata.shortDescription:
"Why sell, Dad? Rent it out and let it pay you every month!" Sam's house is paid off, worth $600,000, and could rent for $3,000 a month. So should he become a landlord, or sell and invest the money? We ran the real numbers.

You'll learn:
• The real costs of renting out a house: taxes, landlord insurance, repairs, vacancy, turnover and property management
• Why $36K a year in rent can shrink to about $17K
• How rental income is taxed, and how depreciation works
• Selling and investing vs. keeping the house: the full comparison
• The 3-year window to keep the home sale tax break
• Depreciation recapture: the tax that comes back when you sell
• How inheriting a rental can wipe out the tax for your kids
• What being a landlord really involves: screening, deposits and the law
• When renting makes sense, when selling does, and how Ben made it work with a low-rate mortgage

0:13 Lily's question
0:33 What the rent really leaves you: property tax
0:51 Landlord insurance
1:02 Repairs
1:15 Vacancy
1:32 Turnover costs and HOA rules
1:48 Property managers

These are example numbers. Rental, tax and landlord rules vary by state and city. This video is for general information only and is not tax, legal or financial advice. Talk to a tax professional and a local attorney before you decide.

Subscribe to House Math for real estate and homebuying, explained with simple numbers.

metadata.shortDescription:
How do you turn a midterm rental portfolio into a $100K/month business while serving your community during times of crisis? In this episode, we sit down with KP Akom, a U.S. Army veteran and the CEO of Streamlined Stay Solutions, to uncover his incredible journey from creative financing deals to filling 100 FEMA housing requests during Hurricane Helene.

KP shares how he leverages Furnished Finder’s Housing Request feature to secure high-value government and insurance contracts, how he tests markets with rental arbitrage before purchasing, and why midterm rentals are the ultimate niche for savvy investors. Whether you're curious about scaling with subject-to deals, managing properties across multiple markets, or thriving in the midterm rental, corporate housing space, this episode is packed with actionable insights. KP owns and operates over 40 properties on Furnished Finder, making him an expert in this space.

metadata.title: Relocation Housing Explained: Where to Stay When Your New Home Isn't Ready
metadata.author: Mid Term Rental Properties
metadata.shortDescription:
Starting a new job in a new city, but your new home isn't ready yet? This 3-minute explainer covers relocation housing: what it is, why employees and families need temporary furnished accommodation during a move, what it usually includes, how long it lasts, who pays for it, and how to choose between corporate apartments, furnished homes, extended-stay hotels and short-term rentals.

Relocation housing is temporary, usually furnished accommodation that gives employees and families a comfortable place to stay while they move into a permanent home. It bridges the gap when a home purchase is still closing, a new lease hasn't started, visa or work permit paperwork is still processing, or family members are arriving later. It's a useful guide for relocating employees, families moving to a new city or country, HR professionals and corporate relocation coordinators.

Chapters
0:00 New job, new city, but where will you live?
0:12 What is relocation housing?
0:29 Why people need temporary housing
0:52 What relocation housing includes
1:16 How long relocation housing lasts
1:37 Who pays for relocation housing?
1:58 Choosing the right temporary housing
2:19 Where Mid Term Rental Properties (MTRP) comes in
2:45 Take the next step

What you'll learn
• Common reasons for temporary housing: job relocation and transfers, waiting for a home purchase or a new lease, visa and work permit processing, house hunting, and family members arriving later
• What furnished relocation housing may include: furnished living spaces, an equipped kitchen, utilities and Wi-Fi, laundry facilities, comfortable bedrooms and convenient locations, depending on the property
• How long it lasts: 30 to 90 days is common, and longer stays may be possible. Duration varies by employer and relocation arrangement, so confirm the stay period and whether extensions are possible.
• Who pays: employer-paid accommodation, a temporary housing allowance, approved expense reimbursement or other relocation package benefits. Confirm your budget, payment arrangements, included services and extension policies before you move.
• How to choose: weigh family size, length of stay, budget, location and lifestyle

Mid Term Rental Properties (MTRP) connects individuals, families and corporate housing partners with furnished accommodation options across the United States and Canada for stays of 30 days or longer.

Find your stay:
🌐 https://midtermrentalproperties.com
✉️ stay@midtermrentalproperties.com
Follow @midtermrentalproperties on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and LinkedIn for more housing insights.

Availability, pricing and included amenities vary by property and location.

#RelocationHousing #TemporaryHousing #CorporateHousing

In this video, we give real estate investors a starting point before they shop for co-living insurance: why standard landlord policies often do not fit a rent-by-the-room house, what can happen when the policy does not match the property, the vocabulary you need, the coverage to ask about, where to look, and how to check every answer for yourself.

At ALE Housing, we provide convenient and comfortable temporary housing solutions for insurance policyholders and families in need of short-term rentals. Whether you’ve experienced property damage or require Alternative Living Expense (ALE) housing, our team makes it easy to find fully furnished, move-in-ready homes that fit your needs.

We specialize in:

Temporary housing for insurance claims
ALE housing solutions for displaced families
Short-term furnished rentals for emergencies or home repairs
Let ALE Housing handle the details—so you can focus on getting back to normal. We work directly with insurance companies to secure quality alternative housing solutions quickly and efficiently.

Contact ALE Housing today or visit our website to discover the best temporary housing and ALE housing solutions available.

metadata.title: What Is Corporate Housing? Hotel vs Rental vs Furnished Stay
metadata.author: Mid Term Rental Properties
metadata.shortDescription:
Need housing for an employee for 30, 60 or even 90 days? A hotel works for a few nights, but longer stays often call for more space, flexibility and the comforts of home. In this 3-minute explainer we cover what corporate housing is, how it compares with hotels and traditional apartment rentals, who uses it, what to look for in a furnished rental, and how to compare the total cost.

Chapters
0:00 Need housing for 30, 60 or 90 days?
0:18 What is corporate housing?
0:36 Hotel vs traditional rental vs corporate housing
0:59 Who needs corporate housing?
1:24 What makes a good corporate rental
1:45 Is corporate housing cheaper than a hotel?
2:07 Meet Mid Term Rental Properties
2:28 Looking for housing or own a furnished rental?
2:47 Get started

What you'll learn
• Corporate housing: furnished accommodation for extended stays, with living space, a kitchen, Wi-Fi and a workspace
• How it fits between hotels (convenient for short trips) and traditional rentals (longer leases, furniture and utility setup)
• Common use cases: employee relocation, temporary work assignments and project teams, insurance-related displacement, and traveling professionals such as travel nurses
• What to check before booking: availability, included utilities, parking, occupancy limits and the terms of the stay
• Why you should compare the total cost (accommodation, taxes, utilities, parking, meals and fees), not just the nightly rate

Mid Term Rental Properties connects property owners and accommodation providers with guests seeking furnished stays of 30 days or longer. Looking for temporary furnished housing, or own a furnished rental you'd like to list for mid-term housing opportunities? 

Whether corporate housing costs less than a hotel depends on the location, property, length of stay and what's included. Actual matches depend on property suitability, location, pricing and guest requirements. Insurance-related housing depends on each policyholder's insurance arrangements.

I give a ton of value for free on how to get started.
